arXiv:2409.18508v2 [math.ST] 27 Jun 2025

Adaptive inference with random ellipsoids through Conformal Conditional Linear Expectation

Iain Henderson ††thanks: iain.henderson@isae-supaero.fr Affiliation: Fédération ENAC ISAE-SUPAERO ONERA, Université de Toulouse, Toulouse, 31055, France    Adrien Mazoyer Affiliation: Institut de Mathématiques de Toulouse, Université de Toulouse, CNRS, UPS, 31062, Toulouse, France    Fabrice Gamboa Affiliation: Institut de Mathématiques de Toulouse, Université de Toulouse, CNRS, UPS, 31062, Toulouse, France
Abstract

We propose two new conformity scores for conformal prediction, in a general multivariate regression framework. The underlying score functions are based on a covariance analysis of the residuals and the input points. We give theoretical guarantees on the prediction sets, which consist in explicit ellipsoids. We study the asymptotic properties of the ellipsoids, and show that their volume is reduced compared to that of classic balls, under ellipticity assumptions. Finally, we illustrate the effectiveness of all our results on an in-depth numerical study, including heavy-tailed as well as non-elliptical distributions.

Keywords

Conformal prediction, distribution free inference, adaptive confidence, confidence ellipsoid

1 Introduction

Uncertainty quantification aims to provide mathematical techniques to quantify uncertainties in computational and real worlds. One very common problem in uncertainty quantification is to provide a confidence set for a given prediction method. When the prediction method is based on a statistical model that is not too complex, classical statistical tools can lead to a confidence set. In black box models, as those developed in machine learning or in complicated regression models the inference process to build such confidence sets is not so straightforward. One now classical way to build such confidence sets stands on a non-parametric learning of the fluctuations of the predictors. This technique called conformal inference allows the construction of a confidence set for a given trained predictor by only observing its behaviour on a calibration sample.

Conformal inference has a long story beginning early in the forty’s by the pioneer works in reliability of Wilks ([51, 52]). Conformal prediction has then been subsequently developed in the early 2000s by a research group around Vapnik and Vovk (see e.g. [49]). With the spectacular progress and the massive implementation of black-box models in neural machine learning, there has been an impressive revival of conformal prediction for at least five or seven years. In a nutshell, conformal prediction is a general concept that includes many different means of providing confidence of pointwise predictions produced using a statistical model or machine learning, without any knowledge on the predictor and under mild assumptions. Indeed, the construction of a prediction set having a high probability of containing a quantity of interest is a general challenging problem in the uncertainty quantification paradigm. More formally, let 𝒳\mathcal{X} and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be some state spaces. Let further (X,Y)∈𝒳×𝒴(X,Y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y} be a random vector. Given a sample (Xi,Yi)i=1,…,n(X_{i},Y_{i})_{i=1,\ldots,n} and a predictor f^:𝒳→𝒴\widehat{f}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} (independent of the sample), for Xn+1∈𝒳X_{n+1}\in\mathcal{X} (a new draw of XX), we aim to build a random measurable region Cαn​(Xn+1)⊆𝒴C_{\alpha}^{n}(X_{n+1})\subseteq\mathcal{Y} as tight as possible, such that for a given α\alpha (close to 00 and set by the user), we have ℙ⁡(Yn+1∈Cαn​(Xn+1))≥1−α.\mathbb{P}\left(Y_{n+1}\in C_{\alpha}^{n}(X_{n+1})\right)\geq 1-\alpha. In some ideal cases, the known statistical properties or characteristics of the predictor f^\widehat{f} can be sole used to construct Cαn​(⋅)C_{\alpha}^{n}(\cdot). However, this usually requires model assumptions on the data, that are sometimes too restrictive or unrealistic. Even worse, it may happen that none of the properties of f^\widehat{f} are useful for building Cαn​(⋅)C_{\alpha}^{n}(\cdot). The aim of Conformal Inference (CI) is to construct such regions, with a very appealing advantage: CI requires only mild assumptions on the sample distribution and on the predictor. Actually, the only hypothesis needed is an exchangeability one, that will be discussed later (see the beginning of Section 2). Roughly speaking, the intuition behind CI is that a relevant prediction for the unknown output Yn+1Y_{n+1} should be any y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} such that (Xn+1,y,f^​(Xn+1))(X_{n+1},y,\widehat{f}(X_{n+1})) seems to be conform to the sample (Xi,Yi,f^​(Xi))i=1,…,n(X_{i},Y_{i},\widehat{f}(X_{i}))_{i=1,\ldots,n}. The main ingredient here is to define and to work with an appropriate score of conformity. Of course, the appropriateness of a given score greatly depends on the context. In particular, the shape and accuracy of the prediction set is directly related both to the performance of the predictor f^\widehat{f} and to the conformity score.

Since its introduction in the early 2000s (see e.g. [50]), conformal prediction has been developed in many different contexts as for example classification [12, 3], regression [29, 7, 43], functional data [13], outlier detection [5, 30], neural networks [41], etc. For more insights and examples, we refer to the recent reviews [28, 2, 17, 24]. In many works dealing with CI, the size and shape of Cαn​(Xn+1)C_{\alpha}^{n}(X_{n+1}) only mildly depend on Xn+1X_{n+1}. This can make sense if for example the covariance of the residual Y−f^​(X)Y-\widehat{f}(X) is homogeneous. Dealing with heterogeneous data can be approached with different objectives in mind. The grail of conformal inference would be to obtain a conditional coverage property for Cαn​(Xn+1)C_{\alpha}^{n}(X_{n+1}), that is ℙ⁡(Yn+1∈Cαn​(Xn+1)|Xn+1)≥1−α\mathbb{P}\left(Y_{n+1}\in C_{\alpha}^{n}(X_{n+1})|X_{n+1}\right)\geq 1-\alpha. However, it is theoretically impossible to ensure the conditional coverage with a finite sample [48]. A less demanding property could be then to be able to capture some geometric features of the conditional distribution ℙ⁡(Y|X)\mathbb{P}(Y|X), typically heteroscedasticity in data. The resulting prediction set should then adapt in terms of shape and size with respect to the input. For example, [28] proposed to use some normalizing statistic in the score, based on the previous sample points. In this last work, the trick consists in normalizing the residuals, for example with respect to their median. Notice furthermore that many of the works in CI consider only the case where 𝒴⊆ℝ\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}, leading thus to prediction intervals. The direct extension to 𝒴⊆ℝℓ\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{\ell} then consists in using a norm of the residual vector R≔Y−f^​(X)R\coloneqq Y-\widehat{f}(X), leading to prediction balls centered on f^​(X)\widehat{f}(X). However, our wish is that the geometry of the prediction set adapts with the input, which cannot be achieved by considering balls. The multidimensional framework is still widely studied, with some ongoing works considering responses taking values in separable metric spaces [32], exploring approaches based on transport tools [54, 45], or formulation in terms of minimum-volume coverage for arbitrary norm-based sets [6].

In this work, we propose and fully investigate CI with a score built on the empirical covariance of (X,Y−f^​(X))(X,Y-\widehat{f}(X)), where both XX and YY are multidimensional. The covariance estimate and score include the prediction point Xn+1X_{n+1} and the potential residual y−f^​(Xn+1)y-\widehat{f}(X_{n+1}). We show that our procedure amounts to estimating the conditional linear expectation of the residual Y−f^​(X)Y-\widehat{f}(X) given the input XX, formulated in a CI setting (see Remark in Section 3.3). We will thus call our method the conformal conditional linear expectation (CCLE). The main advantage of the associated region CαnC_{\alpha}^{n} is that it is well tailored to multivariate outputs Y∈ℝℓY\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}, while remaining easy to compute. Moreover, it leads to adaptive prediction sets in terms of size and shape. It is important to recall that despite the conditional aspect of the score proposed here, its main motivation is not to improve the conditional coverage. Rather, our primary goals are (i)(i) the adaptivity of the prediction set with reference to the distribution of (X,R)(X,R) and (i​i)(ii) decreasing the volume of the prediction set. In Section 4, we discuss the necessary adjustments to recover the conditional coverage in the asymptotic regime.

The following theorem summarises and gives in a nutshell our main results (Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.6, Proposition 4.7, Proposition 4.9 and Proposition 4.10).

Theorem 1.1.

Let ((X1,Y1),…,(Xn+1,Yn+1))((X_{1},Y_{1}),\dots,(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1})) be exchangeable pairs of random vectors and α∈(1/(n+1),1)\alpha\in(1/(n+1),1). Then,

  • •

    There exists explicit 𝓐n,ρn,α\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n},\rho_{n,\alpha} and Y~n+1\widetilde{Y}_{n+1}, only depending on ((X1,Y1),…,(Xn,Yn)),Xn+1((X_{1},Y_{1}),\dots,(X_{n},Y_{n})),\ X_{n+1} and α\alpha, such that the ℓ\ell-dimensional ellipsoid

    Eαn={y∈ℝℓ:(y−Y~n+1)⊤​𝓐n−1​(y−Y~n+1)≤ρn,α}\displaystyle E_{\alpha}^{n}=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}:(y-\widetilde{Y}_{n+1})^{\top}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n}^{-1}(y-\widetilde{Y}_{n+1})\leq\rho_{n,\alpha}\} (1)

    satisfies ℙ⁡(Yn+1∈Eαn)≥1−α.\mathbb{P}(Y_{n+1}\in E_{\alpha}^{n})\geq 1-\alpha.

  • •

    Set R1=Y1−f^​(X1)R_{1}=Y_{1}-\widehat{f}(X_{1}) and assume that (X1,R1)(X_{1},R_{1}) follows an elliptical distribution. Then, as n→+∞n\rightarrow+\infty and under mild assumptions on the distribution of (X1,R1)(X_{1},R_{1}), the volume Vol⁡(Eαn)\mathrm{Vol}(E_{\alpha}^{n}) converges in distribution towards a random variable Vol⁡(Eα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(E_{\alpha}^{\infty}) satisfying

    Vol⁡(Eα∞)≤Vol⁡(Bα∞)​a.s..\displaystyle\mathrm{Vol}(E_{\alpha}^{\infty})\leq\mathrm{Vol}(B^{\infty}_{\alpha})\ a.s.. (2)

    Here, Vol⁡(Bα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(B^{\infty}_{\alpha}) is the (deterministic) limit of the volume of the ball obtained using the standard score ‖Y−f^​(X)‖\|Y-\widehat{f}(X)\| (see Proposition 4.6 for its expression).

In other words, we show that the prediction set obtained using CCLE is an ellipsoid Eαn⊂ℝℓE_{\alpha}^{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{\ell}. Furthermore, the volume of this prediction set is asymptotically smaller than that of the classical conformal prediction ball, under mild ellipticity assumptions (Section 4.3). Elliptical distributions are those whose level sets are elliptical, such as the Gaussian ones. As we will see later, we are actually able to identify two different ρn,α\rho_{n,\alpha} satisfying Theorem 1.1, each with different properties concerning the associated ellipsoid. The first one, corresponding to the joint Mahalanobis score (Section 3.2), leads to ellipsoid EαnE_{\alpha}^{n} such that ℙ⁡(Eαn=∅)>0\mathbb{P}(E_{\alpha}^{n}=\varnothing)>0 and ℙ⁡(Eαn=ℝℓ)=0\mathbb{P}(E_{\alpha}^{n}=\mathbb{R}^{\ell})=0; whereas the second, corresponding to adjusted Mahalanobis score (Section 3.5), leads to ellipsoid FαnF_{\alpha}^{n} such that ℙ⁡(Fαn=∅)=0\mathbb{P}(F_{\alpha}^{n}=\varnothing)=0 and ℙ⁡(Fαn=ℝℓ)>0\mathbb{P}(F_{\alpha}^{n}=\mathbb{R}^{\ell})>0 (this probability tending to 0 as nn tends to ∞\infty). Notably, the second ellipsoid reduces to the conditional prediction set with a minimal volume, in the case of Gaussian data, when nn tends to ∞\infty (Propositions 4.4 and 4.7).

Let us note that to calculate the conditional linear expectation, we will use a ridge estimator for the covariance. This is motivated by three facts. First, it stabilizes the numerical procedure [26], Section 4.4. Secondly, it simplifies several proofs (see e.g. Proposition 3.4). Last but not least, our method will be carried out in an infinite dimensions setting (see [19]) where finite size ellipsoids are rather well-understood (see e.g. Propositions 6.1 to 6.3 in [16]).

Before presenting the outline of our paper, let us further discuss the use of ellipsoidal confidence regions in CI. In [23] and [36] the authors construct local ellipsoidal confidence regions in a standard multivariate CI setting. While our method effectively relies on the conditional linear covariance (see Section 3.3), the local ellipsoids described in [36] correspond to a convex combination of empirical estimates of the global covariance of the residual RR and the true conditional covariance Cov⁡(R|X=x)\mathrm{Cov}(R|X=x) (even though those local ellipsoids are not presented as estimates of Cov⁡(R|X=x)\mathrm{Cov}(R|X=x) in [36]). The latter are estimated by only selecting the observed residuals rir_{i} (realisation of RiR_{i}) such that the corresponding xix_{i} (realisation of XiX_{i}) are the kk closest to the observed realisation xn+1x_{n+1} of Xn+1X_{n+1}. A drawback of this nearest neighbour algorithm is that a sufficient amount of observed inputs xix_{i} close to xn+1x_{n+1} is required to obtain meaningful estimates of Cov⁡(Rn+1|Xn+1=xn+1)\mathrm{Cov}(R_{n+1}|X_{n+1}=x_{n+1}). The authors of [36] then show the practical efficiency of their CI method, but do not further study its theoretical properties. CCLE can also be seen as an intermediate solution between two paradigms: relying on the global (unconditional) covariance matrix Cov⁡(R)\mathrm{Cov}(R), or on the local (fully conditional) covariance matrix Cov⁡(R|X=x)\mathrm{Cov}(R|X=x). CCLE is then an alternative solution to the convex combination proposed in [36]. The recent paper [53] also proposes a CI on the residuals leading also to a confidence ellipsoid. The statistical frame therein is a single realisation of a time series. Here a stationarity assumption is replacing the exchangeability one. The method stands on the estimated empirical covariance of the residuals, estimated from the past. Notice that the method does not encompass any conditional information R|XR|X. The authors show the practical advantage of their method when compared to copula-based CI [35], and establish conditional coverage properties, in the limit of the large observational horizon (this would correspond to the large sample size in our framework). In the case of both [36] and [53], the authors do not study the theoretical properties of the size (volume) of the corresponding confidence regions. We believe that this feature is important in practical applications, along with the conditional coverage. In our work, we study the volumetric properties of EαnE_{\alpha}^{n} in Section 4.3. Finally, in both [36] and [53], the ellipsoids are centered at the predictor f^​(Xn+1)\widehat{f}(X_{n+1}), while our method naturally corrects f^​(Xn+1)\widehat{f}(X_{n+1}) with the empirical conditional linear expectation of RR given XX (Section 3.3 and Proposition 4.5). This feature is interesting as f^\widehat{f} can be biased, which may happen e.g. when f^\widehat{f} is a black-box neural network.

The paper is organized as follows. We recall some preliminaries on split conformal prediction for regression in Section 2. The heart of our work is the Section 3 where we discuss the construction of the conformal score and give some initial results on the induced conformal prediction. This is followed by the Section 4 where we study some asymptotic properties of the conformal ellipsoid, notably its volume under ellipticity assumptions. We illustrate and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our results on simulated data in Section 5. All the technical proofs and technical lemmas are postponed to Appendices B and C.

2 Background for Split Conformal Inference

Let (Ui)i=1,…,n+1(U_{i})_{i=1,\ldots,n+1} be (n+1)(n+1) exchangeable vectors of random variables, with Ui=(Xi,Yi)∈𝒰=𝒳×𝒴U_{i}=(X_{i},Y_{i})\in\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}. This means that the joint distribution of (Ui)i=1,…,n+1(U_{i})_{i=1,\ldots,n+1} is invariant by any permutation of the symmetric group of order (n+1)(n+1). For example, an i.i.d. sample satisfies this assumption. In our framework we assume that (Ui)i=1,…,n(U_{i})_{i=1,\ldots,n}, called the calibration set (or calibration sample), has been observed and that we get Xn+1X_{n+1}. We assume further that we have at hand a predictor f^​(Xn+1)\widehat{f}(X_{n+1}) of Yn+1Y_{n+1}. In this paper, for the sake of simplicity we assume that this predictor is deterministic. For example, it had been built using a sample independent of (Ui)i=1,…,n+1(U_{i})_{i=1,\ldots,n+1} and so we are working conditionally to the training sample (this is the main assumption of split CI, in contrast with full CI where f^\widehat{f} is retrained for each new sample point). The aim is to provide a prediction set for Yn+1Y_{n+1}. More precisely, as discussed in the Introduction, our objective is to construct a conservatively valid prediction set for Yn+1Y_{n+1} with a given level of confidence. Hence, we aim to build a set function CαnC_{\alpha}^{n} defined on (𝒳×𝒴)n×𝒳(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{n}\times\mathcal{X} that will return a measurable subset of 𝒴\mathcal{Y} for Yn+1Y_{n+1} such that

ℙ⁡(Yn+1∈Cαn​((Xi,Yi)i=1​…​n,Xn+1))≥1−α.\mathbb{P}\left(Y_{n+1}\in C_{\alpha}^{n}\left((X_{i},Y_{i})_{i=1\dots n};X_{n+1}\right)\right)\geq 1-\alpha\,. (3)

Notice that in the above probability we have integrated over (Xi,Yi)i=1​…​n+1(X_{i},Y_{i})_{i=1\dots n+1}. The construction of CαnC_{\alpha}^{n} stands on the notion of conformity. To begin with, we define a nonconformity score. It consists in a map SS from 𝒰n×𝒰\mathcal{U}^{n}\times\mathcal{U} to ℝ\mathbb{R}, symmetric in its first nn arguments. The empirical distribution built from (S⁡(U1,…,Un,Uj))j=1,…,n(S(U_{1},\ldots,U_{n};U_{j}))_{j=1,\ldots,n} will be the main tool to quantify how conformal to U1,…,UnU_{1},\ldots,U_{n}, u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} is. Archetypal scores in the usual regression framework with 𝒰=ℝk×ℝℓ\mathcal{U}=\mathbb{R}^{k}\times\mathbb{R}^{\ell} are related to the magnitude of the empirical residual, the most popular example being

S⁡((X1,Y1),…,(Xn,Yn),(x,y))=‖y−f^​(x)‖,S((X_{1},Y_{1}),\dots,(X_{n},Y_{n}),(x,y))=\|y-\widehat{f}(x)\|, (4)

where ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| is the Euclidean norm of ℝℓ\mathbb{R}^{\ell}. Notice that in this last example the score function only depends on u=(x,y)u=(x,y) but not on the calibration sample (U1,…,Un)(U_{1},\ldots,U_{n}). This will not be the case in the framework that we are developing in this paper (see the next section).

Let α∈(1/(n+1),1)\alpha\in(1/(n+1),1). For the sake of conciseness, we will use the notation S⁡(x,y)≔S⁡((X1,Y1),…,(Xn,Yn),(x,y))S(x,y)\coloneqq S((X_{1},Y_{1}),\dots,(X_{n},Y_{n});(x,y)). For i=1,…,n+1i=1,\ldots,n+1, we will also write Si≔S⁡(Xi,Yi)S_{i}\coloneqq S(X_{i},Y_{i}). Following for example [2], the conformalized prediction set for Yn+1Y_{n+1} when observing Xn+1X_{n+1} is then

Cαn​(Xn+1)≡Cαn​((X1,Y1)​…​(Xn,Yn),Xn+1)={y∈𝒴:S⁡(Xn+1,y)≤S(nα)}.C_{\alpha}^{n}(X_{n+1})\equiv C_{\alpha}^{n}((X_{1},Y_{1})\dots(X_{n},Y_{n});X_{n+1})=\left\{y\in\mathcal{Y}\;{:}\;S(X_{n+1},y)\leq S_{(n_{\alpha})}\right\}. (5)

Here, nα≔⌈(1−α)​(n+1)⌉n_{\alpha}\coloneqq\left\lceil(1-\alpha)(n+1)\right\rceil and S(1)≤⋯≤S(n)S_{(1)}\leq\dots\leq S_{(n)} denotes the order statistics associated to (Si)i=1​…​n(S_{i})_{i=1\dots n}. By construction, the above set Cαn​(Xn+1)C_{\alpha}^{n}(X_{n+1}) satisfies

ℙ⁡(Yn+1∈Cαn​(Xn+1))≥1−α.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(Y_{n+1}\in C_{\alpha}^{n}(X_{n+1})\right)\geq 1-\alpha. (6)

The key property ensuring that equation (6) holds is that (Si)i=1,…,n+1(S_{i})_{i=1,\ldots,n+1} is exchangeable. Moreover, if the nonconformity scores (Si)i=1​…​n(S_{i})_{i=1\dots n} have a continuous joint distribution, then we have the following upper bound,

ℙ⁡(Yn+1∈Cαn​(Xn+1))≤1−α+1n+1.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(Y_{n+1}\in C_{\alpha}^{n}(X_{n+1})\right)\leq 1-\alpha+\frac{1}{n+1}\,. (7)

Returning to the regression framework and considering the residual score (4), the prediction set for Yn+1Y_{n+1} given the covariable Xn+1X_{n+1} is

Cαn​(Xn+1)=B⁡(f^​(Xn+1),S(nα)),\displaystyle C_{\alpha}^{n}(X_{n+1})=B\left(\widehat{f}(X_{n+1}),S_{(n_{\alpha})}\right)\,,

i.e. the ball with center f^​(Xn+1)\widehat{f}(X_{n+1}) and radius S(nα)S_{(n_{\alpha})}.

3.2 Joint Mahalanobis score

As discussed in the previous section, a useful score used in CI is the (squared) norm of the residual. In this paper, we will consider a natural generalization of the previous score by considering some statistical evaluation of (R−μR)⊤​𝚺R−1​(R−μR)(R-\mu_{R})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{R}^{-1}(R-\mu_{R}) (assuming that everything here is well defined). Before explaining how we will estimate and handle the previous quantity, let it first bulk up by including XX in the score. For this purpose, let V≔(X⊤​R⊤)⊤∈ℝpV\coloneqq(X^{\top}\ R^{\top})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and set

𝒮=(V−μV)⊤​𝚺V−1​(V−μV).\displaystyle\mathcal{S}=(V-\mu_{V})^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1}_{V}(V-\mu_{V}). (8)

As before, we assume here that everything is well defined. The intuition behind this score is to work with standardized quantities. One may recognize in (8) the so-called Mahalanobis quadratic form, which in turn defines the Mahalanobis metric. This metric is classical in multivariate analysis and widely used for example for classification tasks (see [33]). The idea of including the covariate XX in the score is inspired by the CI framework for time series, where XX can contain the kk previous residuals (see e.g. [31], Section 4.2, or the end of this subsection) : the joint distribution (X⊤​R⊤)⊤(X^{\top}R^{\top})^{\top} is relevant for predicting the future ℓ\ell residuals (i.e. RR).

In the context of CI, the position and covariance parameters of VV are of course unknown or even undefined, and it is natural to replace them with their empirical estimators. Nevertheless, in order to preserve exchangeability and so the finite sample theoretical guarantees provided by the classical CI procedure, one has to process such empirical estimators in an exchangeable fashion. Of course, another way to proceed would be to estimate these parameters separately, similarly to the pre-trained predictor, leading to a double split procedure. The first option is more challenging and this is our approach here. To begin with, we now introduce precisely our working score. We first set

Vi=(XiRi)⁡(i=1,…,n)​ and, for ​z∈ℝℓ,Vn+1​(z)=(Xn+1z).V_{i}=\begin{pmatrix}X_{i}\\ R_{i}\end{pmatrix}\;(i=1,\ldots,n)\mbox{ and, for }z\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell},\;V_{n+1}(z)=\begin{pmatrix}X_{n+1}\\ z\end{pmatrix}. (9)

Here, the variable z=y−f^​(Xn+1)z=y-\widehat{f}(X_{n+1}) (resp. yy) is used to locate the most likely potential residuals (resp. predictions) in the CI machinery. We store the observation vectors Vi,i=1​…,nV_{i},\;i=1\ldots,n and the guess Vn+1​(z)V_{n+1}(z) in a matrix 𝐕⁡(z)∈ℳn+1,p\mathbf{V}(z)\in\mathcal{M}_{n+1,p} whose first nn row are the Vi⊤,i=1,…,nV_{i}^{\top},i=1,\ldots,n and the last one is Vn+1⊤​(z)V_{n+1}^{\top}(z). Following equation (9), we decompose 𝐕⁡(z)\mathbf{V}(z) as 𝐕⁡(z)=(𝐗​𝐑​(z))\mathbf{V}(z)=(\mathbf{X}\ \mathbf{R}(z)) with 𝐗∈ℳn+1,k\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{M}_{n+1,k} and 𝐑⁡(z)∈ℳn+1,ℓ\mathbf{R}(z)\in\mathcal{M}_{n+1,\ell}. The empirically centered counterpart of 𝐕⁡(z)\mathbf{V}(z) is 𝐖⁡(z)=π𝟙⟂​𝐕​(z)\mathbf{W}(z)=\pi^{\perp}_{\mathbbm{1}}\mathbf{V}(z). We further compute the ridge empirical covariance matrix 𝚺^λ​(z)∈ℳp,p\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{\lambda}(z)\in\mathcal{M}_{p,p},

𝚺^λ​(z)=1n​𝐖​(z)⊤​𝐖​(z)+λ​𝐈.\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{\lambda}(z)=\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{W}(z)^{\top}\mathbf{W}(z)+\lambda\mathbf{I}. (10)

Here, λ>0\lambda>0 is the ridge parameter. With all these supplementary notations, we are now able to define the score Si​(z)​(1≤i≤n+1)S_{i}(z)\;(1\leq i\leq n+1) as the square of the empirical Mahanalobis norm of Wi​(z)W_{i}(z) (the ithi^{\mathrm{th}} row of 𝐖⁡(z)\mathbf{W}(z) written in column). Namely, we have

Si(z)=∥𝚺^λ−1/2(z)Wi(z)∥2=Wi(z)⊤𝚺^λ−1(z)Wi(z).\displaystyle S_{i}(z)=\|\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{\lambda}^{-1/2}(z)W_{i}(z)\|^{2}=W_{i}(z)^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{\lambda}^{-1}(z)W_{i}(z). (11)

It is readily seen that Si​(z)S_{i}(z) is the i​thi\textsuperscript{th} diagonal element of the following matrix,

𝐒⁡(z)\displaystyle\mathbf{S}(z) =𝐖⁡(z)​(1n​𝐖​(z)⊤​𝐖​(z)+λ​𝐈)−1​𝐖​(z)⊤\displaystyle=\mathbf{W}(z)\bigg(\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{W}(z)^{\top}\mathbf{W}(z)+\lambda\mathbf{I}\bigg)^{-1}\mathbf{W}(z)^{\top}
=n​𝐖​(z)​(𝐖​(z)⊤​𝐖​(z)+n​λ​𝐈)−1​𝐖​(z)⊤.\displaystyle=n\mathbf{W}(z)\Big(\mathbf{W}(z)^{\top}\mathbf{W}(z)+n\lambda\mathbf{I}\Big)^{-1}\mathbf{W}(z)^{\top}. (12)

Remarkably, and contrarily to the norm residual score, the first nn scores (S1​(z),…,Sn​(z))(S_{1}(z),\ldots,S_{n}(z)) also depend on zz. This property induces a number of technical difficulties which are dealt with in Section 3.4. To alleviate the notations we will sometimes omit the dependence in zz in the matrix valued functions.

First intuition on the confidence regions associated to S⁡(z)S(z)

Before continuing with the main results, let us consider the Gaussian case (X⊤​R⊤)⊤∼𝒩⁡(0,Σ)(X^{\top}R^{\top})^{\top}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma). Anticipating Section 4, we replace the ridge empirical covariance with Σ\Sigma and set λ=0\lambda=0. Then, setting T⁡(z)=z−Σ21​Σ11−1​XT(z)=z-\Sigma_{21}\Sigma_{11}^{-1}X with z=y−f^​(X)z=y-\widehat{f}(X) and using the block inversion lemma (equation (90)), our score amounts to

S⁡(z)\displaystyle S(z) =(Xz)⊤​𝚺−1​(Xz)=X⊤​(𝚺11)−1​X+T​(z)⊤​(𝚺/𝚺11)−1​T​(z).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}X\\ z\end{pmatrix}^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}X\\ z\end{pmatrix}=X^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}X+T(z)^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}T(z). (13)

Assume also that the quantile of order 1−α1-\alpha of S⁡(R)S(R) (denoted by q1−αℰq_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}) is known, so that we can replace the empirical quantile usually computed in CI by its theoretical value q1−αℰq_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}. The confidence region becomes

ℰα∞\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} ={z:X⊤​(𝚺11)−1​X+T​(z)⊤​(𝚺/𝚺11)−1​T​(z)≤q1−αℰ}.\displaystyle=\{z:X^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}X+T(z)^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}T(z)\leq q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}\}. (14)

Under our Gaussianity assumption, q1−αℰ=q1−α​(χ2​(p))q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}=q_{1-\alpha}(\chi^{2}(p)). The ellipsoid ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} has two important features : it is centered on the conditional expectation 𝔼⁡[R|X]=Σ21​Σ11−1​X\mathbb{E}[R|X]=\Sigma_{21}\Sigma_{11}^{-1}X and its matrix is equal to the conditional covariance Cov⁡(R|X)=𝚺/𝚺11\mathrm{Cov}(R|X)=\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11}. However, we can see in this simple case that ℰα∞=∅⇔X⊤​(𝚺11)−1​X≥q1−αℰ\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}=\varnothing\iff X^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}X\geq q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}. This observation suggests the introduction of S′​(z)S^{\prime}(z), an adjusted version of the score S⁡(z)S(z), defined as

S′​(z)=S⁡(z)−X⊤​(𝚺11)−1​X=T​(z)⊤​(𝚺/𝚺11)−1​T​(z).S^{\prime}(z)=S(z)-X^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}X=T(z)^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}T(z). (15)

The score S′S^{\prime} is studied in Section 3.5. This new score leads to a second confidence region

ℱα∞={z:T​(z)⊤​(𝚺/𝚺11)−1​T​(z)≤q1−αℱ},\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty}=\{z:T(z)^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}T(z)\leq q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}}\}, (16)

where q1−αℱ=q1−α​(χ2​(ℓ))q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}}=q_{1-\alpha}(\chi^{2}(\ell)) in the Gaussian case. Contrarily to ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}, this region is never empty as Σ21​Σ11−1​X∈ℱα∞\Sigma_{21}\Sigma_{11}^{-1}X\in\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty}. In return, its finite sample counterpart ℱαn\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{n} can equal to ℝℓ\mathbb{R}^{\ell} (Section 3.5). Observe finally that when working with the score matrix (12), it is not obvious anymore that the prediction region built with the score matrix (12) is an ellipsoid, although we expect to obtain a prediction set similar to ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}.

Computation of the score

Let us comment the effective computation of equation (12) before stating the upcoming Theorem 3.1. The evaluation of 𝐒⁡(z)\mathbf{S}(z) in (12) is not directly tractable: for each candidate zz, both a matrix inversion and matrix products have to be performed. Fortunately, it turns out that explicit inversion tricks can be used to overcome this first issue. First, notice that the matrix 𝐕⁡(z)\mathbf{V}(z) is a linear function of zz. More explicitly, we may write 𝐕⁡(z)=𝐕⁡(0)+𝐀⁡(z)\mathbf{V}(z)=\mathbf{V}(0)+\mathbf{A}(z), where 𝐀⁡(z)\mathbf{A}(z) is the rank one matrix given by

𝐀⁡(z)=en+1​(∑s=1ℓzs​ek+s)⊤=en+1​(𝐋​z)⊤,\displaystyle\mathbf{A}(z)=e_{n+1}\bigg(\sum_{s=1}^{\ell}z_{s}e_{k+s}\bigg)^{\top}=e_{n+1}(\mathbf{L}z)^{\top}, (17)

where 𝐋∈ℳp,ℓ\mathbf{L}\in\mathcal{M}_{p,\ell} is the matrix such that 𝐋⊤=(𝟎ℓ,k𝐈ℓ)\mathbf{L}^{\top}=(\mathbf{0}_{\ell,k}\ \vline\ \mathbf{I}_{\ell}). Thus,

𝐖⁡(z)=π𝟙⟂​𝐕​(0)+π𝟙⟂​en+1​(𝐋​z)⊤=𝐖⁡(0)+v​(𝐋​z)⊤.\displaystyle\mathbf{W}(z)=\pi^{\perp}_{\mathbbm{1}}\mathbf{V}(0)+\pi^{\perp}_{\mathbbm{1}}e_{n+1}(\mathbf{L}z)^{\top}=\mathbf{W}(0)+v(\mathbf{L}z)^{\top}. (18)

Here,

v=π𝟙⟂​en+1=en+1−1n+1​𝟙=1n+1​(−1−1​…−1​n)⊤,with‖v‖2=nn+1.\displaystyle v=\pi^{\perp}_{\mathbbm{1}}e_{n+1}=e_{n+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\mathbbm{1}=\frac{1}{n+1}(-1-1\ldots-1\ n)^{\top},\ \ \ \text{with}\ \ \ \|v\|^{2}=\frac{n}{n+1}. (19)

Equation (18) shows that 𝐖⁡(z)\mathbf{W}(z) is a rank one perturbation of 𝐖⁡(0)\mathbf{W}(0). This crucial property is exploited in Lemma B.2, to prove our main Theorem 3.1.

Remark (Time series framework).

In the context of time series [44, 31], UiU_{i} takes the form Ui=(Uit)t∈ℕU_{i}=(U_{i}^{t})_{t\in\mathbb{N}}. Given a multi-horizon predictor (U^t+1i,…,U^t+ℓi)=f^​(Ut−k+1i,…,Uti)(\widehat{U}_{t+1}^{i},\ldots,\widehat{U}_{t+\ell}^{i})=\widehat{f}(U_{t-k+1}^{i},\ldots,U_{t}^{i}) one then computes the time series of the residuals, Rti=Uti−U^tiR_{t}^{i}=U_{t}^{i}-\widehat{U}_{t}^{i}. At a given time tt, we aim at localizing with high probability the next ℓ\ell residuals, Y=(Rt+1,…,Rt+ℓ)Y=(R_{t+1},\dots,R_{t+\ell}) using the kk previous ones, X=(Rt−k+1,…,Rt)X=(R_{t-k+1},\dots,R_{t}). It may also happen that the time series and so the residuals are both multidimensional (Rs∈ℝdR_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}). This is e.g. the case for time series describing the evolution of a position in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} (d=3d=3). In this case, XX is a vector in ℝk​d\mathbb{R}^{kd} and YY as a vector in ℝℓ​d\mathbb{R}^{\ell d}. The vector corresponding to the i​thi\textsuperscript{th} time series takes the form

Vi=(Xi⊤​Yi⊤)⊤∈ℝd​k+d​ℓ.\displaystyle V_{i}=(X_{i}^{\top}\ Y_{i}^{\top})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{dk+d\ell}. (20)

This time series setting falls in the framework of this paper and will be developed extensively in [18].

The most direct interpretation of the score vector diag​(𝐒⁡(z))=(S1​(z),…,Sn+1​(z))\text{diag}(\mathbf{S}(z))=(S_{1}(z),\ldots,S_{n+1}(z)) is the empirical Mahalanobis distance. This metric is e.g. also the central tool in linear discriminant analysis (LDA) [39], Chapter 9-10. This is closely related to the Karhunen-Loève decomposition, which consists in finding an orthonormal basis (ξi⊗ϕi)i∈ℕ⊂L2​(ℙ)⊗L2​(ℝd)(\xi_{i}\otimes\phi_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{N}}\subset L^{2}(\mathbb{P})\otimes L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) on which a random field is naturally decomposed. It is worth to notice that other interpretations in terms of leverage score and shape theory can also be made. The interested reader will find some insights in Appendix A.1.

3.3 The first ellipsoid ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} : main theorem

We first need to introduce some notations. While the score 𝐒⁡(z)\mathbf{S}(z) is built on a procedure which is exchangeable in the (n+1)(n+1)-sample, we will in fact need quantities that are obtained only using the nn sample (V1,…,Vn)(V_{1},\dots,V_{n}). For this, we introduce the matrices 𝐁n∈ℳn,p\mathbf{B}_{n}\in\mathcal{M}_{n,p}, 𝚺^n,λ∈ℳp,p\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}\in\mathcal{M}_{p,p} and 𝐏n,λ∈ℳn,n\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda}\in\mathcal{M}_{n,n} such that

(𝐁n)i​j\displaystyle(\mathbf{B}_{n})_{ij} ≔(Vi)j−1n​∑k=1n(Vk)j,𝚺^n,λ≔1n​𝐁n⊤​𝐁n+λ​𝐈p=(𝚺^n,λ11𝚺^n12𝚺^n21𝚺^n,λ22),\displaystyle\coloneqq(V_{i})_{j}-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}(V_{k})_{j},\ \ \widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}\coloneqq\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{B}_{n}^{\top}\mathbf{B}_{n}+\lambda\mathbf{I}_{p}=\begin{pmatrix}\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}^{11}&\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n}^{12}\\ \widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n}^{21}&\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}^{22}\end{pmatrix}, (21)
𝐏n,λ\displaystyle\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda} ≔𝐁n​(𝐁n⊤​𝐁n+n​λ​𝐈p)−1​𝐁n⊤=1n​𝐁n​𝚺^n,λ−1​𝐁n⊤.\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbf{B}_{n}(\mathbf{B}_{n}^{\top}\mathbf{B}_{n}+n\lambda\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}\mathbf{B}_{n}^{\top}=\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{B}_{n}\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}^{-1}\mathbf{B}_{n}^{\top}. (22)

Above, 𝚺^n,λ11∈ℳk,k,𝚺^n,λ22∈ℳℓ,ℓ,𝚺^n12∈ℳk,ℓ,\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}^{11}\in\mathcal{M}_{k,k},\ \widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}^{22}\in\mathcal{M}_{\ell,\ell},\ \widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n}^{12}\in\mathcal{M}_{k,\ell}, and 𝚺^n21=(𝚺^n12)⊤∈ℳℓ,k\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n}^{21}=(\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n}^{12})^{\top}\in\mathcal{M}_{\ell,k}. 𝐁n\mathbf{B}_{n} contains the data of the nn-sample after being centered with their empirical mean, and 𝚺^n,λ\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda} is the corresponding empirical ridge covariance matrix. The matrix 𝐏n,λ\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda} is a regularized orthogonal projector, that is, 𝐏n,0\mathbf{P}_{n,0} is an orthogonal projector, 𝐏n,λ⊤=𝐏n,λ\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda}^{\top}=\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda} and 0≼𝐏n,λ≼𝐏n,00\preccurlyeq\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda}\preccurlyeq\mathbf{P}_{n,0} for λ>0\lambda>0. Denoting pi,n=(𝐏n,λ)i​ip_{i,n}=(\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda})_{ii} (pi,n∈[0,1]p_{i,n}\in[0,1]) we set

qn,α≔n​p(nα),\displaystyle q_{n,\alpha}\coloneqq np_{(n_{\alpha})}, (23)

the nαthn^{\text{th}}_{\alpha} order statistic of the nn-tuple (n​p1,n,…,n​pn,n)(np_{1,n},\dots,np_{n,n}). Note that p(nα)p_{(n_{\alpha})} is the empirical quantile of order (1−α)​(n+1)/n(1-\alpha)(n+1)/n for the nn-tuple (p1,n,…,pn,n)(p_{1,n},\dots,p_{n,n}), and not 1−α1-\alpha (apply e.g. [47], p. 305). Contrarily to standard nn-samples, the pi,np_{i,n} are not independent. For example, they are constrained by the following deterministic inequality: ∑i=1npi,n=Tr⁡(𝐏n,λ)≤Tr⁡(𝐏n,0)=rank​(𝐏n,0)≤p\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i,n}=\mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda})\leq\mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf{P}_{n,0})=\text{rank}(\mathbf{P}_{n,0})\leq p.

We can now state our first main result.

Theorem 3.1.

Let α∈(1/(n+1),1)\alpha\in(1/(n+1),1). let ((X1,Y1),…,(Xn+1,Yn+1))((X_{1},Y_{1}),\dots,(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1})) ∈(𝒳×𝒴)n+1\in(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{n+1} exchangeable pairs of random vectors. If qn,α≥n−1q_{n,\alpha}\geq n-1, we set ℰαn≔ℝℓ\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}\coloneqq\mathbb{R}^{\ell}. If qn,α<n−1q_{n,\alpha}<n-1, we define ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} as the following ellipsoid,

ℰαn={z∈ℝℓ:(z−Z0n)⊤​𝓐n−1​(z−Z0n)≤ρn,α},\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}:(z-Z_{0}^{n})^{\top}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n}^{-1}(z-Z_{0}^{n})\leq\rho_{n,\alpha}\}, (24)

𝓐n\displaystyle\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n} =𝚺^n,λ/𝚺^n,λ11,\displaystyle=\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}/\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}^{11}, (25)
Z0n\displaystyle Z_{0}^{n} =𝚺^n21​(𝚺^n,λ11)−1​Xn+1c+R¯n,\displaystyle=\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n}^{21}(\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}^{11})^{-1}X_{n+1}^{\mathrm{c}}+\overline{R}_{n}, (26)
ρn,α\displaystyle\rho_{n,\alpha} =qn,α+11−(qn,α+1)/n−1−(Xn+1c)⊤​(𝚺^n,λ11)−1​Xn+1c.\displaystyle=\frac{q_{n,\alpha}+1}{1-(q_{n,\alpha}+1)/n}-1-(X_{n+1}^{\mathrm{c}})^{\top}(\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}^{11})^{-1}X_{n+1}^{\mathrm{c}}. (27)

Then the set ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} satisfies

ℙ⁡(Yn+1−Y^n+1∈ℰαn)≥1−α.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(Y_{n+1}-\widehat{Y}_{n+1}\in\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n})\geq 1-\alpha. (28)

The ellipsoid in Theorem 1.1 is recovered by Eαn={Y^n+1}+ℰαnE_{\alpha}^{n}=\{\widehat{Y}_{n+1}\}+\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}, in the sense of the usual Minkowski set addition.

An important feature of Lemma B.3 is that 𝓐n\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n} does not depend on Vn+1V_{n+1}. Likewise, ρn,α\rho_{n,\alpha} and Z0nZ_{0}^{n} depend on Vn+1V_{n+1} only through Xn+1X_{n+1}. Interestingly, when the distribution of V1V_{1} is elliptical (see Section 4.3) and V1V_{1} admits second order moment, the matrix 𝓐n\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n} corresponds to an empirical estimate of the conditional covariance matrix Cov⁡(R1|X1)\mathrm{Cov}(R_{1}|X_{1}), up to a random positive multiplicative constant (see [39], Theorem 1.5.4). In fact, one can see from equation (24) that only ρn,α​𝓐n\rho_{n,\alpha}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n} is uniquely defined. This allows us to interpret 𝓐n\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n} as an empirical conditional covariance matrix for such distributions, up to a rescaling of ρn,α\rho_{n,\alpha} with the said multiplicative constant.

Remark (Empirical linear conditional expectation).

Observe that Z0n=e^n+𝐀^n​Xn+1Z_{0}^{n}=\widehat{e}_{n}+\widehat{\mathbf{A}}_{n}X_{n+1}, where

𝐀^n=𝚺^n21​(𝚺^n,λ11)−1,e^n=R¯n−𝐀^n​X¯n.\displaystyle\widehat{\mathbf{A}}_{n}=\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n}^{21}(\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}^{11})^{-1},\ \ \widehat{e}_{n}=\overline{R}_{n}-\widehat{\mathbf{A}}_{n}\overline{X}_{n}. (29)

Interestingly, it is easily shown that (e^n,𝐀^n)(\widehat{e}_{n},\widehat{\mathbf{A}}_{n}) is an M-estimator obtained by minimizing

Tn​(e,𝐀)=1n​∑i=1n‖Ri−e−𝐀​Xi‖2+λ​‖𝐀‖F2,\displaystyle T_{n}(e,\mathbf{A})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|R_{i}-e-\mathbf{A}X_{i}\|^{2}+\lambda\|\mathbf{A}\|_{F}^{2}, (30)

which simply corresponds to ridge multivariate linear regression. The continuous counterpart of TnT_{n} is T⁡(e,𝐀)=𝔼⁡[‖R−e−𝐀​X‖2]+λ​‖𝐀‖F2T(e,\mathbf{A})=\mathbb{E}[\|R-e-\mathbf{A}X\|^{2}]+\lambda\|\mathbf{A}\|_{F}^{2}, which is minimal for 𝐀∗=𝚺21​(𝚺λ11)−1\mathbf{A}_{*}=\bm{\Sigma}^{21}(\bm{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{11})^{-1} and e∗=𝔼⁡[R1]−𝐀∗​𝔼​[X1]e_{*}=\mathbb{E}[R_{1}]-\mathbf{A}_{*}\mathbb{E}[X_{1}]. The pair (e∗,A∗)(e_{*},A_{*}) yields the best affine approximation of RR in terms of XX, in the sense of L2​(ℙ)L^{2}(\mathbb{P}), and the resulting affine map is known as the linear conditional expectation ([26], e.g. Theorem 4.14). In comparison, the (full) conditional expectation is obtained by minimizing the map T⁡(f)=𝔼⁡[‖R−f⁡(X)‖2]T(f)=\mathbb{E}[\|R-f(X)\|^{2}] over all measurable maps ff. Finally, 𝓐n\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n} and (e^n,𝐀^n)(\widehat{e}_{n},\widehat{\mathbf{A}}_{n}) are linked together by min⁡Tn=Tn​(e^n,𝐀^n)=Tr⁡(𝓐n)−ℓ​λ\min T_{n}=T_{n}(\widehat{e}_{n},\widehat{\mathbf{A}}_{n})=\mathrm{Tr}(\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n})-\ell\lambda.

In the previous theorem, the introduced objects are not exchangeable in terms of the (n+1)(n+1)-sample. Netherveless, we will show in next section how the ellipsoid ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} can be exchangeably rewritten.

3.4 From the score matrix 𝐒⁡(z)\mathbf{S}(z) to the ellipsoid ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}

An important first step consists in rewriting the score matrix 𝐒⁡(z)\mathbf{S}(z), using the fact that 𝐖⁡(z)\mathbf{W}(z) can be written as a rank-one perturbation (see eq. (18)). Applying then Lemma B.2 to 𝐒⁡(z)\mathbf{S}(z), we obtain that 𝐒⁡(z)\mathbf{S}(z) is of the form

𝐒⁡(z)\displaystyle\mathbf{S}(z) =n​𝐂n−n​bn​(z)​bn​(z)⊤1+dn​(z).\displaystyle=n\mathbf{C}_{n}-n\frac{b^{n}(z)b^{n}(z)^{\top}}{1+d_{n}(z)}. (31)

Detailed expressions of 𝐂n,bn​(z)\mathbf{C}_{n},b^{n}(z) and dn​(z)d_{n}(z) are given in Lemma B.4. Notably, the vector bn​(z)b^{n}(z) is affine in zz and dn​(z)d^{n}(z) is a positive quadratic form in zz. Recall that we are interested in the diagonal terms (𝐒⁡(z))i​i(\mathbf{S}(z))_{ii}, hereinafter denoted by Si​(z)S_{i}(z) for short. Equation (31) implies that the evaluation of the full score vector (S1​(z),…,Sn+1​(z))(S_{1}(z),\ \ldots\ ,S_{n+1}(z)) requires only one matrix inversion (𝐃μ−1\mathbf{D}_{\mu}^{-1}, see Lemma B.2), instead of one inversion per zz candidate if using formula (12). The second step consists in applying Lemma B.3, which shows that 𝐂n\mathbf{C}_{n} in equation (31) is given by

𝐂n=(𝐏n,λ𝟎n,1𝟎1,n0)+w​w⊤∈ℳn+1,n+1,w≔v‖v‖.\displaystyle\mathbf{C}_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda}&\mathbf{0}_{n,1}\\ \mathbf{0}_{1,n}&0\end{pmatrix}+ww^{\top}\in\mathcal{M}_{n+1,n+1},\ \ \ w\coloneqq\frac{v}{\|v\|}\,. (32)

Here, 𝐏n,λ\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda} is given in equation (22). In particular, for i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\}, (𝐂n)i​i=pi,n+1/n⁡(n+1)(\mathbf{C}_{n})_{ii}=p_{i,n}+1/n(n+1). In fact, 𝐂n\mathbf{C}_{n} does not depend on Vn+1V_{n+1}, while dn​(z)d_{n}(z) and bn​(z)b^{n}(z) only depend on Vn+1V_{n+1} through Xn+1X_{n+1}.

Note that up until now, the expression for the score 𝐒⁡(z)\mathbf{S}(z) is exact. However, a limitation remains: the scores Si​(z)S_{i}(z) of the first nn examples also depend on z=y−Y^n+1z=y-\widehat{Y}^{n+1}. In particular, the conformal region CαnC_{\alpha}^{n} for our score is Cαn={Y^n+1}+𝒞αnC_{\alpha}^{n}=\{\widehat{Y}_{n+1}\}+\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}^{n}, where

𝒞αn={z∈ℝℓ:Sn+1​(z)≤S(nα)​(z)}.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}^{n}=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}:S_{n+1}(z)\leq S_{(n_{\alpha})}(z)\}. (33)

Here, S(nα)​(z)S_{(n_{\alpha})}(z) is the nαthn^{\text{th}}_{\alpha} order statistic of the nn-tuple (S1​(z),…,Sn​(z))(S_{1}(z),\dots,S_{n}(z)). As such, the computation of the region 𝒞αn\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}^{n} still requires that the scoring rule be tested for each y∈𝒴trialy\in\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{trial}}. To alleviate this second computational difficulty, a simple approximation of the confidence region is given by the next lemma.

Lemma 3.2 (Conservative approximation of 𝒞αn\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}^{n}).

Let α∈(1/(n+1),1)\alpha\in(1/(n+1),1). Introduce the set 𝒞~αn\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{\alpha}^{n}, defined as

𝒞~αn≔{z∈ℝℓ:Sn+1​(z)≤qn,α+1n+1}.\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{\alpha}^{n}\coloneqq\bigg\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}:S_{n+1}(z)\leq q_{n,\alpha}+\frac{1}{n+1}\bigg\}. (34)

Before commenting Lemma 3.2 above, we can already state our main result, which completes the proof of Theorem 3.1.

Proposition 3.3.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 3.1, 𝒞~αn=ℰαn\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{\alpha}^{n}=\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}.

The approximation given in equation (34) corresponds to discarding the contribution bn​(z)​bn​(z)⊤b^{n}(z)b^{n}(z)^{\top} in Si​(z)S_{i}(z) for i≠n+1i\neq n+1 in equation (31), observing that Si​(z)≤n​(𝐂n)i​iS_{i}(z)\leq n(\mathbf{C}_{n})_{ii} uniformly in zz. Assume that the ViV_{i} are iid, that λ>0\lambda>0 and that 𝔼⁡[‖V1‖4​q]<+∞\mathbb{E}[\|V_{1}\|^{4q}]<+\infty for some q>1q>1. Then for all compact set K⊂ℝℓK\subset\mathbb{R}^{\ell},

Vol⁡((ℰαn∖𝒞αn)∩K)→n→∞ℙ0.\displaystyle\mathrm{Vol}\big((\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}^{n})\cap K\big)\xrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{\mathbb{P}}0. (35)

The interested reader will find in Appendix A.2 discussions on the settings of the above Proposition, in particular the case λ=0\lambda=0 and the finite 4​q4q-th moment assumption.

We conclude this section with the following lemma, which provides a sufficient condition on nn and p=k+ℓp=k+\ell so that full space ellipsoids (ℰαn=ℝℓ\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}=\mathbb{R}^{\ell}) never occur.

Lemma 3.5 (Sufficient condition for bounded ellipsoids).

For all λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, we have qn,α<n−1q_{n,\alpha}<n-1 almost surely as soon as n>p+1n>p+1 and

α≥p+1n+1.\displaystyle\alpha\geq\frac{p+1}{n+1}. (36)

A sharper bound, where λ\lambda and max⁡Spec⁡(𝚺^n,λ)\max\mathrm{Spec}(\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}) appear, can be obtained by writing an SVD of 𝐏n,λ\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda}. Equation (36) is to be compared with the standard requirement in conformal inference that α>1/(n+1)\alpha>1/(n+1). Note also that n+1n+1 and pp are the number of rows and columns of 𝐕\mathbf{V}, respectively. In practice, we observe that qn,α<n−1q_{n,\alpha}<n-1 may hold even if p+1≥np+1\geq n, the proof of Lemma 3.5 being a worst-case analysis.

Metrics of the ellipsoid

An important metric related to the shape of an ellipsoid is its principal eccentricity. Given an ellipsoid ℰ={z∈ℝℓ:(z−z0)​𝓐−1​(z−z0)≤1}\mathcal{E}=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}:(z-z_{0})\bm{\mathcal{A}}^{-1}(z-z_{0})\leq 1\}, this corresponds to

e=1−λm/λM∈[0,1),\displaystyle e=\sqrt{1-\lambda_{m}/\lambda_{M}}\in[0,1), (37)

where λm\lambda_{m} is the smallest eigenvalue of 𝓐\bm{\mathcal{A}} and λM\lambda_{M} is the largest one. Roughly speaking, this metric measures how “different” is a given ellipsoid from a ball, the latter corresponding to e=0e=0. Likewise, if ee is close to 11 then ℰ\mathcal{E} is accordingly flat. The volume of ℰ\mathcal{E} above is

Vol​(ℰ)=vℓ​det(𝓐),wherevℓ=πℓ/2/Γ⁡(ℓ/2+1).\displaystyle\text{Vol}(\mathcal{E})=v_{\ell}\sqrt{\det(\bm{\mathcal{A}})},\quad\text{where}\quad v_{\ell}={\pi^{\ell/2}}/{\Gamma({\ell}/{2}+1)}. (38)

Here, vℓv_{\ell} corresponds to the volume of the ℓ\ell-dimensional unit ball. In our case, the determinant of 𝓐n\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n} can be further computed as (see e.g. [20], Section 0.8.5)

det(𝓐n)\displaystyle\det(\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n}) =det(𝚺^n,λ/𝚺^n,λ11)=det(𝚺^n,λ)/det(𝚺^n,λ11).\displaystyle=\det\big(\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}/\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}^{11}\big)=\det\big(\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}\big)/\det\big(\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda}^{11}\big). (39)

Case where ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} is empty

Empty confidence regions ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} correspond to ρn,α<0\rho_{n,\alpha}<0. This event has a non-null probability, as e.g. visible from equation (55) (still, ℙ⁡(ℰαn=∅)≤α\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}=\varnothing)\leq\alpha by construction). To understand the event {ℰαn=∅}\{\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}=\varnothing\}, observe that ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} can be written as ℰαn=𝒱⁡(Xn+1)∩ℰ\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}=\mathcal{V}(X_{n+1})\cap\mathcal{E}, where 𝒱⁡(Xn+1)\mathcal{V}(X_{n+1}) is an ℓ\ell-dimensional affine subspace of ℝk+ℓ\mathbb{R}^{k+\ell} and ℰ\mathcal{E} is a (k+ℓ)(k+\ell)-dimensional ellipsoid. They are given by, for some explicit βn>0\beta_{n}>0,

𝒱⁡(Xn+1)\displaystyle\mathcal{V}(X_{n+1}) ≔{v=(x⊤​r⊤)⊤∈ℝk+ℓ:x=Xn+1},\displaystyle\coloneqq\{v=(x^{\top}r^{\top})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{k+\ell}:x=X_{n+1}\},
ℰ\displaystyle\mathcal{E} ≔{v∈ℝk+ℓ:(v−V¯n)⊤​(𝚺^n,λ)−1​(v−V¯n)≤βn},V¯n=1n​∑i=1nVi.\displaystyle\coloneqq\{v\in\mathbb{R}^{k+\ell}:(v-\overline{V}_{n})^{\top}(\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,\lambda})^{-1}(v-\overline{V}_{n})\leq\beta_{n}\},\ \ \overline{V}_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}V_{i}.

(to obtain ℰ\mathcal{E}, combine equations (125) and (126)). In this setting, ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} is empty precisely when 𝒱⁡(Xn+1)∩ℰ=∅\mathcal{V}(X_{n+1})\cap\mathcal{E}=\varnothing. This is interpreted as Xn+1X_{n+1} being so abnormal (w.r.t. the score S⁡(z)S(z)) that no value of zz can make the pair (Xn+1⊤​z⊤)⊤(X_{n+1}^{\top}\ z^{\top})^{\top} conform to the samples (V1,…,Vn)(V_{1},\ldots,V_{n}). While this is unexpected from a UQ perspective, this is natural in the context of outlier detection : Xn+1X_{n+1} is so abnormal that (Xn+1⊤​z⊤)⊤(X_{n+1}^{\top}\ z^{\top})^{\top} is always an outlier, whatever the value of zz.

Empty confidence regions can be problematic from an applied perspective. Moreover, empty ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} are not devoid of information, since 𝓐n\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n} and Z0nZ_{0}^{n} are still defined when ρn,α<0\rho_{n,\alpha}<0. (z−Z0n)⊤​(ρn,αε​𝓐n)−1​(z−Z0n)\displaystyle(z-Z_{0}^{n})^{\top}(\rho_{n,\alpha}^{\varepsilon}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n})^{-1}(z-Z_{0}^{n}) ≤1.\displaystyle\leq 1. (40)

ε\varepsilon is found by solving Vmin=vℓ​det(ρn,αε​𝓐n)=vℓ​εℓ​det(𝓐n)V_{\min}=v_{\ell}\sqrt{\det(\rho_{n,\alpha}^{\varepsilon}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n})}=v_{\ell}{\varepsilon}^{\ell}\sqrt{\det(\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n})}, i.e.

ε=(Vmin/(vℓ​det(𝓐n)1/2))1/ℓ.\displaystyle\varepsilon=\Big(V_{\min}/\big(v_{\ell}\det(\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n})^{1/2}\big)\Big)^{1/\ell}. (41)

By construction, this procedure leads to overcoverage, but if VminV_{\min} is chosen small enough (e.g. if Vmin≪𝔼⁡[Vol⁡(ℰαn)]V_{\min}\ll\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n})]), it will not affect the empirical average volume of the confidence ellipsoid ℰα,εn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha,\varepsilon}^{n}, since the cutoff ρε=max⁡(ρ,ε2)\rho_{\varepsilon}=\max(\rho,\varepsilon^{2}) is only activated when the volume of ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} is very small or null.

A more mathematically sound way of avoiding empty regions is found by using the score S′​(z)S^{\prime}(z) introduced below.

Observe that a large dnXd_{n}^{X} means that Xn+1X_{n+1} is far away from X¯n\overline{X}_{n}, in the data metric 𝚺n,λ\mathbf{\Sigma}_{n,\lambda}. In the second case, this is interpreted as the whole calibration sample (V1,…,Vn)(V_{1},\ldots,V_{n}) being uninformative with reference to the current sample (Xn+1⊤​Rn+1⊤)⊤(X_{n+1}^{\top}\ R_{n+1}^{\top})^{\top}, when the new input Xn+1X_{n+1} is too abnormal when compared to (X1,…,Xn)(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}).

    𝓐n\displaystyle\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n} →n→∞a.s.𝓐∞≔𝚺λ/𝚺λ11,\displaystyle\xlongrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{a.s.}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty}\coloneqq\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}/\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{11}, (51)
    ρn,α\displaystyle\rho_{n,\alpha} →n→∞dρ∞,α≔q1−αℰ−Xc⊤​(𝚺λ11)−1​Xc,\displaystyle\xlongrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{\mathrm{d}}\rho_{\infty,\alpha}\coloneqq q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}-X_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\big(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{11}\big)^{-1}X_{\mathrm{c}}, (52)
    Z0n\displaystyle Z_{0}^{n} →n→∞dZ0∞≔𝚺21​(𝚺λ11)−1​Xc+𝔼⁡[R1].\displaystyle\xlongrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{\mathrm{d}}Z_{0}^{\infty}\coloneqq\mathbf{\Sigma}^{21}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{11})^{-1}X_{\mathrm{c}}+\mathbb{E}[R_{1}]. (53)
  2. 2.

    (Asymptotic volume and probability of empty regions)

    Vol⁡(ℰαn)\displaystyle\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}) →n→∞dvℓ​det(𝚺λ/𝚺λ11)​(q1−αℰ−Xc⊤​(𝚺λ11)−1​Xc)+ℓ/2,\displaystyle\xlongrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{\mathrm{d}}v_{\ell}\sqrt{\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}/\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{11})}\big(q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}-X_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{11})^{-1}X_{\mathrm{c}}\big)^{\ell/2}_{+}, (54)
