Finally, if 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} is invertible, then all the results above remain true when λ=0\lambda=0.

In equation (54), we underline that (x)+s=max⁡(0,x)s≠max⁡(0,xs)(x)_{+}^{s}=\max(0,x)^{s}\neq\max(0,x^{s}); in particular, (x)+s=0(x)_{+}^{s}=0 if x≤0x\leq 0. We now define the random ellipsoid ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} as

ℰα∞≔{z∈ℝℓ:(z−Z0∞)⊤​𝓐∞−1​(z−Z0∞)≤ρ∞,α}.\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}\coloneqq\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}:(z-Z_{0}^{\infty})^{\top}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty}^{-1}(z-Z_{0}^{\infty})\leq\rho_{\infty,\alpha}\}. (56)

Observe that ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} is a confidence region of level 1−α1-\alpha for R1R_{1}: from equation (90) and the expressions of 𝓐∞\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty}, Z0∞Z_{0}^{\infty} and ρ∞,α\rho_{\infty,\alpha}, we can show that (see equations (171) and (172))

Vc⊤​𝚺λ−1​Vc≤q1−αℰ⇔(Rc−Z0∞)⊤​𝓐∞−1​(Rc−Z0∞)≤ρ∞,α,\displaystyle V_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{-1}V_{\mathrm{c}}\leq q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}\iff(R_{\mathrm{c}}-Z_{0}^{\infty})^{\top}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty}^{-1}(R_{\mathrm{c}}-Z_{0}^{\infty})\leq\rho_{\infty,\alpha}, (57)

and the left-hand side has probability 1−α1-\alpha from the definition of q1−αℰq_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}. Next, the distribution of the volume Vol⁡(ℰα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}) volume is equal to that of the right-hand side of (54). In this paper, we do not tackle the question of random set convergence, i.e in what sense does the convergence ℰαn→ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} hold. This study would require the use of random set theory [38], a perspective that we leave for future work.

Note that the limit volume Vol⁡(ℰα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}) is bounded almost surely, hence all its moments are finite (equation (75)). However, there is no guarantee that the moments of Vol⁡(ℰαn)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}) converge toward those of Vol⁡(ℰα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}). Such a property requires additional uniform integrability properties on Vol⁡(ℰαn)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}), which have to be checked on a case-by-case basis. For example, this property holds in the Gaussian case (Proposition 4.2). The main obstacle in the proof of Proposition 4.1 is that of the convergence of the empirical quantile qn,αq_{n,\alpha} to q1−αℰq_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}, as the diagonal elements of 𝐂n\mathbf{C}_{n} are not independent. Our proof of this result relies on the study of empirical characteristic functions and an almost sure application of Lévy’s theorem (Lemma B.6). Note that the asymptotic matrix 𝓐∞\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty} is the covariance matrix of πX⟂​R\pi^{\perp}_{X}R, where πX⟂​R\pi^{\perp}_{X}R is the orthogonal projection of R=(R1,…,Rℓ)R=(R_{1},\dots,R_{\ell}) onto [Span⁡(X1,…,Xk)]⟂[\mathrm{Span}(X_{1},\dots,X_{k})]^{\perp} in L2​(ℙ)L^{2}(\mathbb{P}).

It is worth noticing that the numerical experiments highlight that the asymptotic ellipsoid (as well as its volume) may still exist when the data are heavy tailed. A starting point to study that case is to note that, according to equation (24), the region ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} is mostly determined by the product ρn,α​𝓐n\rho_{n,\alpha}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n}. Then scalings differing from the one used in Proposition 4.1 (i.e. (ρn,α/un)​(un​𝓐n)(\rho_{n,\alpha}/u_{n})(u_{n}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n}) with un≠1u_{n}\neq 1) may be introduced, in the hope that un​𝓐nu_{n}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n} and ρn,α/un\rho_{n,\alpha}/u_{n} may converge in some sense. The interested reader will find first insights in Appendix A.3 for a further study of heavy-tailed data.

Remark (Conditional coverage).

Although our method is built on a form of conditional procedure, it cannot fulfill the conditional coverage described in the introduction, even when n→∞n\rightarrow\infty. Indeed, if X1=xX_{1}=x, then ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} is empty as soon as q1−αℰ<(x−𝔼⁡[X1])⊤​(𝚺11)−1​(x−𝔼⁡[X1])q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}<(x-\mathbb{E}[X_{1}])^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}(x-\mathbb{E}[X_{1}]) (Proposition 4.1). In particular, for all such xx,

ℙ⁡(R1∈ℰα∞|X1=x)=ℙ⁡(R1∈∅|X1=x)=0≠1−α.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(R_{1}\in\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}|X_{1}=x)=\mathbb{P}(R_{1}\in\varnothing|X_{1}=x)=0\neq 1-\alpha. (58)

To recover conditional coverage, the asymptotic quantile q1−αℰ=q1−α​(Vc⊤​𝚺−1​Vc)q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}=q_{1-\alpha}(V_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1}V_{\mathrm{c}}) should be replaced with q1−αℰ​(x)≔q1−α​(Vc⊤​𝚺−1​Vc|X1=x)q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}(x)\coloneqq q_{1-\alpha}(V_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1}V_{\mathrm{c}}|X_{1}=x) in equation (52). Indeed, let us define

ρ∞,α​(x)≔q1−αℰ​(x)−(x−𝔼⁡[X1])⊤​(𝚺11)−1​(x−𝔼⁡[X1]),\displaystyle\rho_{\infty,\alpha}(x)\coloneqq q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}(x)-(x-\mathbb{E}[X_{1}])^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}(x-\mathbb{E}[X_{1}]), (59)

and define ℰα∞​(x)\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}(x) to be the set ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} where ρ∞,α\rho_{\infty,\alpha} has been replaced with ρ∞,α​(x)\rho_{\infty,\alpha}(x). Then, from equation (172), we recover conditional coverage in the limit where n→∞n\rightarrow\infty:

ℙ⁡(R1∈ℰα∞​(x)|X=x)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(R_{1}\in\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}(x)|X=x) =ℙ⁡((Rc−Z0∞)⊤​𝓐∞−1​(Rc−Z0∞)≤ρ∞,α​(x)|X1=x)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}((R_{\mathrm{c}}-Z_{0}^{\infty})^{\top}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty}^{-1}(R_{\mathrm{c}}-Z_{0}^{\infty})\leq\rho_{\infty,\alpha}(x)|X_{1}=x)
=ℙ⁡(Vc⊤​𝚺λ−1​Vc≤q1−αℰ​(x)|X1=x)=1−α.\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(V_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{-1}V_{\mathrm{c}}\leq q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}(x)|X_{1}=x)=1-\alpha. (60)

This solution also solves the problem of empty confidence regions described in Section 3. Of course, the main difficulty is that of the estimation of the conditional quantile q1−α​(x)q_{1-\alpha}(x). This can be done e.g. using conformalized quantile regression [43], although the application of this method has to be further studied in our case.

Gaussian data

In this paragraph, we assume that V1V_{1} is a Gaussian random vector. In this case, Z0∞=𝔼⁡[R1|X1]Z_{0}^{\infty}=\mathbb{E}[R_{1}|X_{1}] and 𝓐∞=Cov⁡(R1|X1)\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty}=\mathrm{Cov}(R_{1}|X_{1}). In fact, the limit ellipsoid ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} is an ℓ\ell-dimensional section of the k+ℓk+\ell-dimensional confidence ellipsoid obtained under Gaussianity assumptions over the random vector (X1,R1)(X_{1},R_{1}) (this is also true under general ellipticity assumptions, see equation (71) for a definition). CCLE can thus be understood as a “non asymptotic conformal generalisation” of the regions provided by standard Gaussian ellipsoids. In the Gaussian case, we can further describe the volume of ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} when λ=0\lambda=0, notably its moments.

Proposition 4.2.

Assume that the vectors ViV_{i} are iid, the vector V1V_{1} is Gaussian, λ=0\lambda=0 and min⁡Spec⁡(𝚺)>0\min\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbf{\Sigma})>0. Denoting Fχ2​(m)F_{\chi^{2}(m)} the CDF of the χ2​(m)\chi^{2}(m) distribution, we have q1−αℰ=Fχ2​(k+ℓ)−1​(1−α)q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}=F^{-1}_{\chi^{2}(k+\ell)}(1-\alpha). Next, denoting B⁡(x,y)B(x,y) the Euler Beta function, we set Ck,ℓ,q≔2−k/2vℓqB(k/2,qℓ/2+1)/Γ(k/2)C_{k,\ell,q}\coloneqq 2^{-k/2}v_{\ell}^{q}B({k}/{2},{q\ell}/{2}+1)/\Gamma(k/2). Then for all q>0q>0,

𝔼⁡[Vol​(ℰαn)q]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n})^{q}] →n→∞𝔼⁡[Vol​(ℰα∞)q]=Ck,ℓ,q​det(𝚺/𝚺11)q/2​(q1−αℰ)(k+q​ℓ)/2​F11​(k2,k+q​ℓ2+1,−q1−αℰ2),\displaystyle\xrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{}\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty})^{q}]=C_{k,\ell,q}\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{q/2}(q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}})^{(k+q\ell)/2}{{}_{1}F_{1}}\bigg(\frac{k}{2},\frac{k+q\ell}{2}+1,-\frac{q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}}{2}\bigg), (61)
ℙ⁡(ℰαn=∅)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}=\varnothing) →n→∞ℙ⁡(ℰα∞=∅)=1−Fχ2​(k)​(Fχ2​(k+ℓ)−1​(1−α)),\displaystyle\xrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{}\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}=\varnothing)=1-F_{\chi^{2}(k)}\Big(F^{-1}_{\chi^{2}(k+\ell)}(1-\alpha)\Big), (62)

where F11{}_{1}F_{1} is the Kummer confluent hypergeometric function of the first kind. In particular,

𝔼⁡[Vol⁡(ℰαn)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n})] →n→∞2−k/2πℓ/2Γ⁡(p/2+1)​det(𝚺/𝚺11)1/2​(q1−αℰ)p/2​F11​(k2,p2+1,−q1−αℰ2).\displaystyle\xlongrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{}\frac{2^{-k/2}\pi^{\ell/2}}{\Gamma(p/2+1)}\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{1/2}(q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}})^{p/2}{{}_{1}F_{1}}\bigg(\frac{k}{2},\frac{p}{2}+1,-\frac{q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}}{2}\bigg). (63)

Formula (61) is empirically verified in Table 1, and Formula (62) is illustrated in Figure 2(b). One may wish to understand the properties of ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} for finite sample size nn. The interested reader will find in Appendix A.4 some discussions on that point, where we identify the distributions of 𝓐n\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n} and dnXd_{n}^{X}, and approximations of those of 𝐏n,0\mathbf{P}_{n,0} and pi,np_{i,n}. However we did not manage to identify that of ρn,α\rho_{n,\alpha}.

4.2 The second asymptotic ellipsoid ℱα∞\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty}

Under the assumptions of Proposition 4.1, the center Z0nZ_{0}^{n} and “matrix” 𝓐n\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n} describing the ellipsoid ℱαn\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{n} obviously still converge to the limits given in equations (51) and (53), as they are the same as those of ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}. The limit of ρn,α′\rho_{n,\alpha}^{\prime} is given in the following proposition.

Proposition 4.3.

Take the assumptions of Proposition 4.1, and set

q1−αℱ≔q1−α​(Tc⊤​𝓐∞−1​Tc),whereTc=Rc−𝚺21​(𝚺λ11)−1​Xc.\displaystyle q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}}\coloneqq q_{1-\alpha}(T_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty}^{-1}T_{\mathrm{c}}),\ \ \text{where}\ \ \ T_{\mathrm{c}}=R_{\mathrm{c}}-\mathbf{\Sigma}^{21}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{11})^{-1}X_{\mathrm{c}}. (64)

If 𝔼⁡[‖X1‖4​q]<+∞\mathbb{E}[\|X_{1}\|^{4q}]<+\infty for some q>1q>1, then

qn,α′\displaystyle q_{n,\alpha}^{\prime} →n→∞ℙq1−αℱ,ρn,α′→n→∞ℙq1−αℱ, and Vol(ℱαn)→n→∞ℙvℓdet(𝚺λ/𝚺λ11)1/2(q1−αℱ)ℓ/2.\displaystyle\xlongrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{\mathbb{P}}q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}},\ \ \ \ \rho_{n,\alpha}^{\prime}\xlongrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{\mathbb{P}}q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}},\ \ \ \ \text{ and }\ \ \ \ \mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{n})\xlongrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{\mathbb{P}}v_{\ell}\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}/\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{11})^{1/2}(q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}})^{\ell/2}. (65)

We denote by ℱα∞\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty} the ellipsoid with center Z0∞Z_{0}^{\infty}, matrix 𝓐∞\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty} and “squared radius” q1−αℱq_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}}. While the convergence of qn,α′q_{n,\alpha}^{\prime} is weaker than that of qn,αq_{n,\alpha}, the convergence of ρn,α′\rho_{n,\alpha}^{\prime} is as strong as that of ρn,α\rho_{n,\alpha} (because the limit of ρn,α′\rho_{n,\alpha}^{\prime} is constant, convergence in probability is equivalent to convergence in distribution).

Observe also that contrarily to Proposition 3.7, we additionally require that 𝔼⁡[‖X1‖4​q]<+∞\mathbb{E}[\|X_{1}\|^{4q}]<+\infty. While this assumption is not necessarily tight, it suggests that the convergence of ℱαn\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{n} towards ℱα∞\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty} may be slower than that of ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} towards ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}, or that it should hold in a weaker sense. This is consistent with the numerical experiments on Cauchy data (Section 5.2).

The remark on the conditional coverage of ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} in the previous section also holds for ℱα∞\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty} if replacing q1−αℱq_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}} with q1−αℱ​(x)≔q1−α​(Tc⊤​𝓐∞−1​Tc|X1=x)q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}}(x)\coloneqq q_{1-\alpha}(T_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty}^{-1}T_{\mathrm{c}}|X_{1}=x). In fact, it is equivalent to estimate q1−αℱ​(x)q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}}(x) or q1−αℰ​(x)q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}(x), as from equation (172),

q1−αℰ​(x)=q1−αℱ​(x)+(x−𝔼⁡[X1])⊤​(𝚺11)−1​(x−𝔼⁡[X1]).\displaystyle q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}(x)=q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}}(x)+(x-\mathbb{E}[X_{1}])^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}(x-\mathbb{E}[X_{1}]).

In particular, ρ∞,α​(x)=q1−αℱ​(x)\rho_{\infty,\alpha}(x)=q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}}(x), and the conditional ellipsoids ℰα∞​(x)\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}(x) and ℱα∞​(x)\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty}(x) are the same. As opposed to ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} though, we recover the conditional coverage for Gaussian data, when using ℱα∞\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty}.

Proposition 4.4.

Assume that V1∼𝒩⁡(m,𝚺)V_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(m,\mathbf{\Sigma}), that min⁡Spec​𝚺>0\min\mathrm{Spec}\mathbf{\Sigma}>0, and set λ=0\lambda=0. Then

∀x∈ℝk,ℙ⁡(Y1−Y^1∈ℱα∞|X1=x)=ℙ⁡(Y1−Y^1∈ℱα∞)=1−α.\displaystyle\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{k},\ \ \ \mathbb{P}(Y_{1}-\widehat{Y}_{1}\in\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty}|X_{1}=x)=\mathbb{P}(Y_{1}-\widehat{Y}_{1}\in\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty})=1-\alpha.

This result is an immediate consequence of the fact that R1−𝚺21​(𝚺11)−1​X1R_{1}-\mathbf{\Sigma}^{21}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}X_{1} is independent from X1X_{1}, when V1V_{1} is Gaussian with Cov⁡(V1)=𝚺\mathrm{Cov}(V_{1})=\mathbf{\Sigma}. Anticipating Section 4.3, this property is unique to Gaussian distributions, among the family of elliptical distributions (see equation (71) for a definition). In the general elliptical case, the conditional distributions R1|X1=xR_{1}|X_{1}=x and R1−𝚺21​(𝚺11)−1​X1R_{1}-\mathbf{\Sigma}^{21}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}X_{1} still have the same dispersion matrix 𝚺/𝚺11\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11}, but they differ in their generator. Coming back to the Gaussian case, numerical evaluations of formula (63) show that if V1V_{1} is Gaussian and λ=0\lambda=0, then on average, ℱα∞\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty} is better than ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} in terms of volume (see Figure 2(c) for a plot) :

∀α∈(0,1),Vol⁡(ℱα∞)≤𝔼⁡[Vol⁡(ℰα∞)].\displaystyle\forall\alpha\in(0,1),\ \ \ \mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty})\leq\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty})]. (66)

It remains possible that Vol⁡(ℰα∞)≤Vol⁡(ℱα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty})\leq\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty}), which corresponds to the event {Xc⊤(𝚺11)−1Xc≥q1−αℰ−q1−αℱ}\{X_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}X_{\mathrm{c}}\geq q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}-q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}}\}.

The corrected predictor

An interesting feature of the ellipsoids for Yn+1Y_{n+1} is that they are not centered at the predictor Y^n+1\widehat{Y}_{n+1}. Their common center is Y~n+1=Z0n+Y^n+1\widetilde{Y}_{n+1}=Z_{0}^{n}+\widehat{Y}_{n+1} which is effectively a correction of Y^n+1\widehat{Y}_{n+1}. In fact, there is no guaranty that Y^n+1\widehat{Y}_{n+1} lies in EαnE_{\alpha}^{n} or FαnF_{\alpha}^{n}, which is desirable as the predictor may e.g. be biased. On the contrary, the next proposition shows that under same moment assumptions as for Proposition 4.1, the corrected predictor Y~n+1\widetilde{Y}_{n+1} is asymptotically unbiased.

Proposition 4.5.

If 𝔼⁡[‖Y1‖]<+∞\mathbb{E}[\|Y_{1}\|]<+\infty then under the assumptions of Proposition 4.1, Y~n+1\widetilde{Y}_{n+1} is asymptotically unbiased, i.e.

𝔼⁡[Y~n+1]→n→∞𝔼⁡[Y1].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{Y}_{n+1}]\xrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{}\mathbb{E}[Y_{1}]. (67)

Moreover, introducing the matrix Mλ≔𝚺λ/𝚺λ11−λ⁡(𝐈ℓ+𝚺21​(𝚺λ11)−2​𝚺12)M_{\lambda}\coloneqq\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}/\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{11}-\lambda(\mathbf{I}_{\ell}+\mathbf{\Sigma}^{21}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{11})^{-2}\mathbf{\Sigma}^{12}), and assuming there exists q>1q>1 such that 𝔼⁡[‖V1‖4​q]<+∞\mathbb{E}[\|V_{1}\|^{4q}]<+\infty, we have the asymptotic covariance and mean squared error,

Cov⁡(Y~n+1−Yn+1)\displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}(\widetilde{Y}_{n+1}-{Y}_{n+1}) →n→∞Mλ,𝔼⁡[‖Y~n+1−Yn+1‖22]→n→∞Tr⁡(Mλ).\displaystyle\xrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{}M_{\lambda},\ \ \ \mathbb{E}\Big[\|\widetilde{Y}_{n+1}-{Y}_{n+1}\|_{2}^{2}\Big]\xrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{}\mathrm{Tr}(M_{\lambda}). (68)

4.3 Comparison with the norm residual score

In regression, the standard score is the norm of the residual, Si′​(y)=‖y−Y^n+1‖S_{i}^{\prime}(y)=\|y-\widehat{Y}_{n+1}\|, where ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| is the Euclidean norm in ℝℓ\mathbb{R}^{\ell}. The corresponding confidence region for Yn+1Y_{n+1} is a ball BαnB_{\alpha}^{n} centered at Y^n+1\widehat{Y}_{n+1}, with squared radius βn,α\beta_{n,\alpha} given by the nαthn^{\text{th}}_{\alpha} order statistic of (‖R1‖2,…,‖Rn‖2)(\|R_{1}\|^{2},\dots,\|R_{n}\|^{2}). As for EαnE_{\alpha}^{n} and ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}, we introduce ℬαn\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{n} the centered ball with squared radius βn,α\beta_{n,\alpha}, so that Bαn={Y^n+1}+ℬαnB_{\alpha}^{n}=\{\widehat{Y}_{n+1}\}+\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{n}. We begin with describing the asymptotic behaviour of ℬαn\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{n}.

Proposition 4.6.

Denote βn,α\beta_{n,\alpha} the nαthn^{\text{th}}_{\alpha} order statistic of (‖R1‖2,…,‖Rn‖2)(\|R_{1}\|^{2},\dots,\|R_{n}\|^{2}), which are assumed iid, and assume that the quantile function of ‖R1‖2\|R_{1}\|^{2} is continuous on a neighbourhood of 1−α1-\alpha. Then

βn,α→a.s.q1−α​(‖R1‖2).\displaystyle\beta_{n,\alpha}\xlongrightarrow{a.s.}q_{1-\alpha}(\|R_{1}\|^{2}). (69)

As a result, the asymptotic volume of the associated ball is deterministic, and given by

Vol⁡(ℬαn)\displaystyle\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{n}) →a.s.vℓ​q1−α​(‖R1‖2)ℓ/2.\displaystyle\xlongrightarrow{a.s.}v_{\ell}q_{1-\alpha}(\|R_{1}\|^{2})^{\ell/2}. (70)

Equation (69) is quite intuitive and natural, though we did not manage to find it stated as such in standard textbooks. We thus provide a proof in the appendix11 1 This proof is a copy of that of Théorème 8.9, p. 90 of the lecture notes [4] (in French).. Similarly to ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}, we define ℬα∞\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty} to be the deterministic ball centered at 00 and with radius q1−α​(‖R1‖)q_{1-\alpha}(\|R_{1}\|). Note that, even in the case of Gaussian residuals, q1−α​(‖R1‖2)q_{1-\alpha}(\|R_{1}\|^{2}) cannot be expected to be further simplified, as ‖R1‖2\|R_{1}\|^{2} would follow a generalized chi-squared distribution.

Elliptical distributions

We can now compare the volumes Vol⁡(ℰα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}) and Vol⁡(ℬα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty}). For this, our main assumption is that the vector V1V_{1} follows an absolutely continuous elliptical distribution. This means that there exists a nonnegative function g:ℝ+→ℝ+g:\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} such that the density ff of V1V_{1} is of the form

f⁡(v)∝g⁡((v−μ)⊤​𝚺−1​(v−μ)),\displaystyle f(v)\propto g((v-\mu)^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1}(v-\mu)), (71)

for some μ∈ℝp\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and 𝚺∈ℳp,p,𝚺≻0\mathbf{\Sigma}\in\mathcal{M}_{p,p},\ \mathbf{\Sigma}\succ 0 ([39], Section 1.5). Above, μ,𝚺\mu,\ \mathbf{\Sigma} and gg are respectively the location parameter, the dispersion matrix and the generator of the distribution (71) (𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} is defined up to a multiplicative constant, which can be absorbed in gg). Elliptical distributions include multivariate Gaussian and Cauchy distributions. Under the assumptions of Proposition 4.1, 𝚺=Cov⁡(V1)\mathbf{\Sigma}=\mathrm{Cov}(V_{1}) up to a deterministic constant ([39], p. 34), although elliptical distributions do not necessarily have finite second order moments. As argued in Appendix A.3, this constant is irrelevant to define ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} (in particular its volume) in an unique way, so that in the rest of this section, we can assume that 𝚺=Cov⁡(V1)\mathbf{\Sigma}=\mathrm{Cov}(V_{1}). This ellipticity assumption is equivalent to the existence of a random vector T=(T1,…,Tp)⊤∈ℝpT=(T_{1},\dots,T_{p})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} with an absolutely continuous spherical distribution, i.e. with a density of the form f⁡(x)=g⁡(‖x‖2)f(x)=g(\|x\|^{2}), such that V1=μ+𝚺1/2​TV_{1}=\mu+\mathbf{\Sigma}^{1/2}T.

We first consider the case where k=0k=0 and λ=0\lambda=0. In this case, 𝚺λ=𝚺=𝚺22\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}=\mathbf{\Sigma}=\mathbf{\Sigma}^{22}, and ℰα∞=ℱα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}=\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty}. Furthermore, denoting λ1,…,λℓ\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{\ell} the eigenvalues of 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma}, we have det(𝚺)=λ1​…​λℓ\det(\mathbf{\Sigma})=\lambda_{1}\dots\lambda_{\ell}. Under such assumptions, Vc⊤​𝚺−1​Vc=∑i=1ℓTi2V_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1}V_{\mathrm{c}}=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}T_{i}^{2} and ‖R1‖2\|R_{1}\|^{2} is equal to ∑i=1ℓλi​(Ti+si)2\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\lambda_{i}(T_{i}+s_{i})^{2} in distribution, for some s=(s1,…,sℓ)⊤∈ℝℓs=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{\ell})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell} (see the upcoming Lemma 4.8 for a more general result). In particular,

(Vol⁡(ℰα∞)Vol⁡(ℬα∞))2/ℓ\displaystyle\bigg(\frac{\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty})}{\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty})}\bigg)^{2/\ell} =det(𝚺)1/ℓ​q1−α​(∑i=1ℓTi2)q1−α​(∑i=1ℓλi​(Ti+si)2)\displaystyle=\det(\mathbf{\Sigma})^{1/\ell}\frac{q_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}T_{i}^{2})}{q_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\lambda_{i}(T_{i}+s_{i})^{2})}
=q1−α​(∑i=1ℓTi2)(λ1⋯λℓ)−1/ℓq1−α(∑i=1ℓλi(Ti+si)2)=q1−α​(∑i=1ℓTi2)q1−α​(∑i=1ℓδi​(Ti+si)2),\displaystyle=\frac{q_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}T_{i}^{2})}{{(\lambda_{1}\cdots\lambda_{\ell})^{-1/\ell}}q_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\lambda_{i}(T_{i}+s_{i})^{2})}=\frac{q_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}T_{i}^{2})}{q_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\delta_{i}(T_{i}+s_{i})^{2})}, (72)

where δi=λi/(λ1⋯λℓ)1/ℓ>0\delta_{i}=\lambda_{i}/(\lambda_{1}\cdots\lambda_{\ell})^{1/\ell}>0 verify δ1⋯δℓ=1\delta_{1}\cdots\delta_{\ell}=1. The comparison of Vol⁡(ℰα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}) and Vol⁡(ℬα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty}) is then settled by the next proposition.

Proposition 4.7.

Let t>0t>0 and (T1,…,Tℓ)(T_{1},\dots,T_{\ell}) be a random vector with an absolutely continuous spherical distribution, i.e. with a density of the form f⁡(x)=g⁡(‖x‖2),x∈ℝℓf(x)=g(\|x\|^{2}),\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}; assume furthermore that gg is non-increasing. For a fixed tt, introduce Ft​(s,δ)≔ℙ⁡(∑i=1ℓδi​(Ti+si)2≤t)F_{t}(s,\delta)\coloneqq\mathbb{P}(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\delta_{i}(T_{i}+s_{i})^{2}\leq t), where s=(s1,…,sℓ)⊤∈ℝℓs=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{\ell})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell} and δ=(δ1,…,δℓ)⊤∈ℝ+ℓ\delta=(\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{\ell})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\ell}. Then

((0,…,0),(1,…,1))∈arg⁡max(s,δ)∈ℝℓ×ℝ+ℓ∏iδi=1​Ft​(s,δ).\displaystyle((0,\ldots,0),(1,\dots,1))\in\underset{\begin{subarray}{c}(s,\delta)\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}^{\ell}\\ \prod_{i}\delta_{i}=1\end{subarray}}{\arg\max}F_{t}(s,\delta)\,. (73)

In particular, when λ=0\lambda=0, k=0k=0 and under the ellipticity assumption (71), Vol⁡(ℰα∞)≤Vol⁡(ℬα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty})\leq\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty}).

The property that the generator gg is nonincreasing is an unimodality assumption (see [10], Definition 3.1.1). Proposition 4.7 relies on the observation that centered balls correspond to level sets of spherical distributions. Note that no moment assumptions are required for equation (73) to hold.

We now consider the case where k≥1k\geq 1, still with λ=0\lambda=0. We start with ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}. Introduce a random vector T=(T1,…,Tp)⊤T=(T_{1},\dots,T_{p})^{\top} with a spherical distribution, such that V1=μ+𝚺1/2​TV_{1}=\mu+\mathbf{\Sigma}^{1/2}T. To compare the volumes of ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} and ℬα∞\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty}, we will need the following lemma which describes the distribution of ‖R1‖2\|R_{1}\|^{2} in terms of that of TT.

Lemma 4.8.

Assume that T∈ℝpT\in\mathbb{R}^{p} has a spherical distribution and V1=μ+𝚺1/2​TV_{1}=\mu+\mathbf{\Sigma}^{1/2}T for some μ∈ℝp\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and 𝚺∈ℳp,p,𝚺≻0\mathbf{\Sigma}\in\mathcal{M}_{p,p},\ \mathbf{\Sigma}\succ 0. Denote (λ1,…,λℓ)(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{\ell}) the eigenvalues of 𝚺22\mathbf{\Sigma}^{22}. Then, there exists s∈ℝℓs\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell} such that we have the equality in distribution

‖R1‖2=d∑i=1ℓλi​(Ti+si)2.\displaystyle\|R_{1}\|^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\lambda_{i}(T_{i}+s_{i})^{2}. (74)

Above, the vector ss is given by s=𝐃−1/2𝐏⊤μs=\mathbf{D}^{-1/2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\mu, where 𝚺22=𝐏𝐃𝐏⊤\mathbf{\Sigma}^{22}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{P}^{\top} is an eigendecomposition of 𝚺22\mathbf{\Sigma}^{22}. To compare Vol⁡(ℰα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}) and Vol⁡(ℬα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty}), we will mimic the case k=0k=0 (see equation (72)). To do so, we will require the bound

0≤(q1−αℰ−Xc⊤​(𝚺11)−1​Xc)+≤q1−αℰ=q1−α​(∑i=1k+ℓTi2)\displaystyle 0\leq(q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}-X_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}X_{\mathrm{c}})_{+}\leq q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}=q_{1-\alpha}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{k+\ell}T_{i}^{2}\bigg) (75)

as well as the ratio cα​(k,ℓ)c_{\alpha}(k,\ell) defined as

cα​(k,ℓ)\displaystyle c_{\alpha}(k,\ell) ≔q1−α​(∑i=1k+ℓTi2)q1−α​(∑i=1ℓTi2)>1.\displaystyle\coloneqq\frac{q_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k+\ell}T_{i}^{2}\right)}{q_{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}T_{i}^{2}\right)}>1. (76)

From these two equations as well as Proposition 4.7 and Lemma 4.8, we are able to prove Proposition 4.9 below.

Proposition 4.9.

Denote the dependence of ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} on λ\lambda as ℰα,λ∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha,\lambda}^{\infty}. Under the assumptions of Proposition 4.1, if

cα​(k,ℓ)​(det(𝚺/𝚺11)det(𝚺22))1/ℓ≤1,\displaystyle c_{\alpha}(k,\ell)\bigg(\frac{\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})}{\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{22})}\bigg)^{1/\ell}\leq 1, (77)

then Vol⁡(ℰα,0∞)≤Vol⁡(ℬα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha,0}^{\infty})\leq\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty}). Moreover, if the inequality in equation (77) is strict, then there exists λ0>0\lambda_{0}>0 such that for all λ∈[0,λ0]\lambda\in[0,\lambda_{0}], Vol⁡(ℰα,λ∞)≤Vol⁡(ℬα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha,\lambda}^{\infty})\leq\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty}). Finally, λ0\lambda_{0} can be chosen as the unique solution to the algebraic equation

det(𝚺λ0)=cα​(k,ℓ)−ℓ​det(𝚺λ011)​det(𝚺22).\displaystyle\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda_{0}})=c_{\alpha}(k,\ell)^{-\ell}\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda_{0}}^{11})\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{22})\,. (78)

The condition (77) can be relaxed to having the first part of equation (202) smaller than one. The algebraic equation for finding λ0\lambda_{0} is correspondingly changed as

det(𝚺λ0)=(q1−α​(∑i=1k+ℓTi2)q1−α​(∑i=1ℓδi​(Ti+si)2))−ℓ​det(𝚺λ011)​det(𝚺22).\displaystyle\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda_{0}})=\Bigg(\frac{q_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{i=1}^{k+\ell}T_{i}^{2})}{q_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\delta_{i}(T_{i}+s_{i})^{2})}\Bigg)^{-\ell}\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda_{0}}^{11})\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{22}). (79)

The condition (77) enables to identify two distinctive features of the data, when aiming at optimizing the volume of ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}: the intrinsic distribution of the TiT_{i} and the values of kk and ℓ\ell on the one hand, and the structure of 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} on the other hand. In particular it shows that in order to minimize the volume of ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}, we are faced with a tradeoff when using many explanatory variables. As kk increases, the determinant of the Schur complement decreases (this can be seen from the block inversion lemma), but the ratio cα​(k,ℓ)c_{\alpha}(k,\ell) increases at the same time. This tradeoff is illustrated in Section 5.1 (Table 2).

Remark (Optimal choice of explanatory variables).

In view of this tradeoff, a natural question is that of the selection of the best variables within X1X_{1} to explain the response variable R1R_{1}, especially if kk is large. For example, if R1R_{1} is independent of (X1)1(X_{1})_{1}, the first coordinate of X1X_{1}, then taking it into account will not decrease the determinant of the Schur complement, as (when λ=0\lambda=0) it is equal to the conditional covariance Cov⁡(R1|X1)\mathrm{Cov}(R_{1}|X_{1}). It will, however, increase the ratio cα​(k,ℓ)c_{\alpha}(k,\ell), thus increasing the volume of ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}. Likewise, if (X1)1=(X1)2(X_{1})_{1}=(X_{1})_{2}, then only one of those random variables is required to explain R1R_{1}. In our context, this question boils down to that of the research of active subspaces, which is e.g. studied in [11]. The use of active subspace methods in our framework is left for future work.

To deal with the case k≥1k\geq 1, we used the bound (75), which may seem very conservative. This is not entirely true, in the following sense. Setting S=Xc⊤​(𝚺11)−1​XcS=X_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}X_{\mathrm{c}}, the expected volume 𝔼⁡[Vol​(ℰα∞)]\mathbb{E}[\text{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty})] is given by 𝔼⁡[(q1−αℰ−S)+ℓ/2]=(q1−αℰ)ℓ/2​𝔼​[(1−S/q1−αℰ)+ℓ/2]\mathbb{E}[(q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}-S)_{+}^{\ell/2}]=(q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}})^{\ell/2}\mathbb{E}[(1-S/q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}})_{+}^{\ell/2}], up to a deterministic constant. Assuming that q1−αℰ→+∞q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}\rightarrow+\infty when α→0+\alpha\rightarrow 0^{+}, we then deduce from the bound 0≤(1−S/q)+≤1​(q>0)0\leq(1-S/q)_{+}\leq 1\ (q>0) and the dominated convergence theorem that

𝔼⁡[(q1−αℰ−Xc⊤​(𝚺11)−1​Xc)+ℓ/2]​∼α→0+​(q1−αℰ)ℓ/2.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}}-X_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}X_{\mathrm{c}})_{+}^{\ell/2}]\underset{\alpha\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\sim}(q_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{E}})^{\ell/2}. (80)

In particular, the right-hand side in equation (80) corresponds to the bound one would obtain using the conservative bound (75).

Remark (Conditional coverage for elliptical distributions).

If the distribution of V1V_{1} is elliptical, it is possible to obtain the conditional distribution R1|X1R_{1}|X_{1} from the observation of β↦qβ​(Vc⊤​𝚺−1​Vc)\beta\mapsto q_{\beta}(V_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1}V_{\mathrm{c}}), as we can deduce the spherical density gg appearing in equation (71) from this quantile map. For all xx, using the definition of the conditional density and the knowledge (or estimates) of g,μg,\mu and 𝚺\bm{\Sigma}, one can do derive the conditional distribution R|X=xR|X=x, and q1−α​(Vc⊤​𝚺−1​Vc|X1=x)q_{1-\alpha}(V_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\bm{\Sigma}^{-1}V_{\mathrm{c}}|X_{1}=x) in particular, in integral/implicit form. As remarked in Section 4.1, this conditional quantile is the required quantity to recover conditional coverage using our methodology. The use of this observation in a practical setting is left for future work.

Contrarily to ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}, the case k≥1,λ=0k\geq 1,\lambda=0 is easily dealt with for ℱα∞\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty}.

Proposition 4.10.

Set λ=0\lambda=0, and assume that V1V_{1} follows and elliptical distribution with a non-increasing generator g:ℝ+→ℝ+g:\mathbb{R}^{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+}. Then we have, almost surely,

Vol⁡(ℱα∞)≤Vol⁡(ℬα∞).\displaystyle\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty})\leq\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty}). (81)

The key to Proposition 4.10 is the observation that Tc⊤​𝓐∞−1​Tc=d∑i=1ℓTi2T_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty}^{-1}T_{\mathrm{c}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}T_{i}^{2}. This fact can be used together with Lemma 4.8 and Proposition 4.7 to obtain the desired result. As opposed to Proposition 4.9, the dependence on kk of the asymptotic volume of ℱα∞\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty} is milder than that of ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}, when V1V_{1} is elliptical. In particular, minimizing Vol⁡(ℱα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty}) as a function of kk is equivalent to minimizing the determinant

det(𝚺/𝚺11)=det(𝚺22−𝚺21​(𝚺11)−1​𝚺12),\displaystyle\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})=\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{22}-\mathbf{\Sigma}^{21}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}\mathbf{\Sigma}^{12}), (82)

which can be shown to be a decreasing function of kk using the block-inversion lemma. Thus, one can only hope the this quantity becomes stationary for large kk, and large values of kk (a form of complexity) are not penalised, contrarily to ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}.

Non elliptical distributions

In this paragraph, we assume that k=0k=0 and λ=0\lambda=0, so that 𝚺λ=𝚺=𝚺22=Cov⁡(R1)\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}=\mathbf{\Sigma}=\mathbf{\Sigma}^{22}=\mathrm{Cov}(R_{1}) and ℰα∞=ℱα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}=\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty}. Without ellipticity assumptions, the comparison of Vol⁡(ℬα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty}) and Vol⁡(ℰα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}) can still be studied for small α\alpha by comparing the tail behaviour of the distributions of ∥𝚺−1/2(R1−𝔼[R1])∥2\|\mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1/2}(R_{1}-\mathbb{E}[R_{1}])\|^{2} and ‖R1‖2/det(𝚺)1/ℓ\|R_{1}\|^{2}/\det(\mathbf{\Sigma})^{1/\ell}. Indeed, if

ℙ(∥𝚺−1/2(R1−𝔼[R1])∥2>t)≤ℙ(∥R1∥2/det(𝚺)1/ℓ>t)for large t,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\|\mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1/2}(R_{1}-\mathbb{E}[R_{1}])\|^{2}>t)\leq\mathbb{P}(\|R_{1}\|^{2}/\det(\mathbf{\Sigma})^{1/\ell}>t)\ \ \ \text{for large $t$}, (83)

then we can show that Vol⁡(ℰα∞)≤Vol⁡(ℬα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty})\leq\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty}) for α\alpha small enough (e.g. adapt the proof of Proposition 4.11, equations (221) and (222)). In this context, the precise decay of the tail distribution of nonnegative random variables is studied in [37], when the decay is either exponential or polynomial. More precisely, [37] proves Tauberian theorems, which link this decay with properties of the Laplace transform of the said distribution. The full use of the results of [37] in our context is left for future work. For the time being we simply observe that, without ellipticity assumptions, it is unreasonable to expect that a scoring rule solely based on a covariance analysis of the residuals will always yield smaller confidence regions than those of the norm residual score. In that sense, the next proposition provides a counterexample for which our method underperforms when compared to the norm residual score. This proposition relies on [37], Theorem 1.2.

Proposition 4.11.

Let λ1,…,λℓ>0\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{\ell}>0 be such that there exists i≠ji\neq j such that λi≠λj\lambda_{i}\neq\lambda_{j}, and define δi≔λi/(λ1⋯λℓ)1/ℓ\delta_{i}\coloneqq\lambda_{i}/(\lambda_{1}\cdots\lambda_{\ell})^{1/\ell}. Then there exists a random vector T∈ℝℓT\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell} with 𝔼⁡[T]=0\mathbb{E}[T]=0 and Cov⁡(T)=𝐈ℓ\mathrm{Cov}(T)=\mathbf{I}_{\ell} such that for large tt,

ℙ⁡(∑i=1ℓTi2>t)>ℙ⁡(∑i=1ℓδi​Ti2>t).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}T_{i}^{2}>t\bigg)>\mathbb{P}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\delta_{i}T_{i}^{2}>t\bigg). (84)

In particular, if R1=𝐃​TR_{1}=\mathbf{D}T where 𝐃\mathbf{D} is diagonal such that 𝐃i​i=λi1/2\mathbf{D}_{ii}=\lambda_{i}^{1/2}, then 𝔼⁡[R1]=0\mathbb{E}[R_{1}]=0, 𝚺=Cov⁡(R1)=𝐃2\mathbf{\Sigma}=\mathrm{Cov}(R_{1})=\mathbf{D}^{2} and for large tt,

ℙ(∥𝚺−1/2R1∥2>t)>ℙ(∥R1∥2/det(𝚺)1/ℓ>t).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\|\mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1/2}R_{1}\|^{2}>t)>\mathbb{P}(\|R_{1}\|^{2}/\det(\mathbf{\Sigma})^{1/\ell}>t). (85)

Thus, if k=0k=0 and λ=0\lambda=0, then for α\alpha small enough , Vol⁡(ℬα∞)<Vol⁡(ℰα∞)\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty})<\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty}).

We see that the inequality (85) is reversed when compared to (83). The vector TT above is built using independent gamma distributions : Ti2∼γ⁡(δi,δi−1)T_{i}^{2}\sim\gamma(\delta_{i},\delta_{i}^{-1}). The proof of Proposition 4.11 relies on the fact that, despite TiT_{i} being centered with unit variance, the tails of Ti2T_{i}^{2} do not decay at the same rate (in particular, the TiT_{i} are not identically distributed). Note that in general, such a property cannot hold if the TiT_{i} are built from a one dimensional family of distributions, as fixing the variance would determine the decay rate. This is the reason why we used general gamma distributions γ⁡(k,θ)\gamma(k,\theta). In the case k≥1k\geq 1, the same counterexample where ℓ\ell is replaced by pp works for ℱα∞\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty}. Indeed, from the independence of the TiT_{i}, 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} is diagonal, hence Z0∞=0Z_{0}^{\infty}=0 a.s., 𝚺/𝚺11=𝚺22\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11}=\mathbf{\Sigma}^{22} and the conclusion of Proposition 4.11 applies. Counter-examples in expectation with ℰα∞\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty} are easily built for α→0+\alpha\rightarrow 0^{+} using centered spherical distributions (μ=0,𝚺=𝑰p\mu=0,\ \bm{\Sigma}=\bm{I}_{p}). Indeed, adapting equation (201) applied to such distributions and using equation (80), we have 𝔼[Vol(ℰα∞)]/Vol(ℬα∞)∼α→0+cα(k,ℓ)ℓ/2>1\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{\infty})]/\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{\infty})\sim_{\alpha\rightarrow 0^{+}}c_{\alpha}(k,\ell)^{\ell/2}>1.

5 Numerical application

The code for generating both data and figures is given in https://github.com/iain-pl-henderson/PyConfCov. The workflow is as follow. We first train the predictor on nsplitn_{\mathrm{split}} data points (Xi,Yi)(X_{i},Y_{i}). Next, for each of the ntestn_{\mathrm{test}} test points, we generate ncalibn_{\mathrm{calib}} calibration points and perform CCLE. By averaging over those ntestn_{\mathrm{test}} experiments, we obtain a realisation of the empirical average volume and coverage of the resulting ellipsoids, denoted by 𝔼^ntest​[Vol⁡(ℰαncalib)]\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n_{\mathrm{test}}}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n_{\mathrm{calib}}})] and 1−𝔼^ntest​[αℰαncalib]1-\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n_{\mathrm{test}}}[\alpha_{\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n_{\mathrm{calib}}}}] (replace ℰαncalib\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n_{\mathrm{calib}}} with ℱαncalib\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{n_{\mathrm{calib}}} if using ℱαncalib\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{n_{\mathrm{calib}}}). We use the same notations for the balls of the norm residual score, replacing ℰ\mathcal{E} with ℬ\mathcal{B} in those notations. We perform this complete procedure (except for the training of the predictor) nhiston_{\mathrm{histo}} times, to obtain a histogram of the distributions of 𝔼^ntest​[Vol⁡(ℰαncalib)]\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n_{\mathrm{test}}}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n_{\mathrm{calib}}})] and 1−𝔼^ntest​[αℰαncalib]1-\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n_{\mathrm{test}}}[\alpha_{\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n_{\mathrm{calib}}}}]. We denote the empirical means of those histograms as 𝔼^nhisto​𝔼^ntest​[Vol⁡(ℰαncalib)]\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n_{\mathrm{histo}}}\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n_{\mathrm{test}}}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n_{\mathrm{calib}}})], and so forth.

5.1 Gaussian data

We consider the case of iid observations of Gaussian random vectors U1,…,Un+1,Ui∈ℝpU_{1},\dots,U_{n+1},\ U_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, where k=6,ℓ=3k=6,\ \ell=3 and p=k+ℓ=9p=k+\ell=9, following a 𝒩⁡(0,𝚺)\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{\Sigma}) distribution. Here, we choose 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} such that 𝚺i,j=k3/2​(i−j)\mathbf{\Sigma}_{i,j}=k_{3/2}(i-j), where kνk_{\nu} is a Matérn covariance function of order ν\nu, with variance σ2=1\sigma^{2}=1 and lengthscale L=5L=5 (see equation (107)). Such a Gaussian vector is a sampling of a centered one dimensional Gaussian process (Ut)t>0(U_{t})_{t>0} at integer grid points {1,…,9}\{1,\dots,9\}, where (Ut)t>0(U_{t})_{t>0} has the said 3/2−3/2-Matérn covariance function. The considered problem is thus that of the simultaneous conformal inference for the ℓ=3\ell=3 next time steps, given the previous k=6k=6 time steps. In the numerical experiments, we will represent the results (U7,U8,U9)(U_{7},U_{8},U_{9}) in (x,y,z)(x,y,z) coordinates.

The 3/23/2-Matérn Gaussian process (Ut)t>0(U_{t})_{t>0} is a continuous AR⁡(2)\mathrm{AR}(2) process, meaning that it is a solution to a second order SDE [42], Appendix B.2. As a consequence, the knowledge of Ut−d​tU_{t-\mathrm{d}t} and UtU_{t} determines the value of Ut+d​tU_{t+\mathrm{d}t} up to a noise of variance of order O⁡(d​t)O(\mathrm{d}t). If the lengthscale LL is large, then the vector (U1,…,U9)(U_{1},\ldots,U_{9}) can be understood as a sampling of the Gaussian vector (Ut)(U_{t}) with a small sampling period TsampleT_{\mathrm{sample}} compared to the characteristic length of the process (Tsample=1≪LT_{\mathrm{sample}}=1\ll L). As such, using our covariance based score, we expect that for large lengthscales LL, U7U_{7} (xx coordinate) will hold low uncertainty, U8U_{8} (yy coordinate) medium uncertainty and U9U_{9} (zz coordinate) will hold most of the uncertainty.

The predictor f^\widehat{f} is obtained by ridge regression trained on previous split data, that is Y^i=β^⊤​Xi\widehat{Y}_{i}=\widehat{\beta}^{\top}X_{i} with β^=(Xs⊤​Xs+μ0​I)−1​Xs⊤​Ys\widehat{\beta}=(X_{\mathrm{s}}^{\top}X_{\mathrm{s}}+\mu_{0}I)^{-1}X_{\mathrm{s}}^{\top}Y_{\mathrm{s}}, where (Xs​Ys)∈ℳnsplit,p(X_{s}\ Y_{\mathrm{s}})\in\mathcal{M}_{n_{\mathrm{split}},p} denotes the training data, stored row-wise. Following the split conformal inference framework, the matrix β^\widehat{\beta} will be considered deterministic in the numerical experiments. All the results correspond to α=0.1\alpha=0.1.

Optimal number of input dimensions kk

In this paragraph, we illustrate the tradeoff principle concerning ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n}, as discussed following Proposition 4.9. we consider a variance σ2=1\sigma^{2}=1 and a lengthscale L=5L=5. Following [42], Section 4.2, Gaussian processes with covariance function kq−1/2k_{q-1/2} are AR⁡(q)\mathrm{AR}(q) processes. As such, we expect the optimal value of kk to be kopt=qk_{\mathrm{opt}}=q. Indeed, seeing the AR⁡(q)\mathrm{AR}(q) relation as a linear recursive sequence of order qq, one should at least use (U6,…,U7−q)(U_{6},\ldots,U_{7-q}) to predict U7U_{7} accurately, and the minimal reasonable value of kk is thus equal to qq. This fact is confirmed by Table 2, which provides empirical estimates of 𝔼⁡[Vol⁡(ℰαn)]\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n})]. Do note that in numerical experiments, especially for q=3q=3 and q=4q=4, it may happen that the optimal value identified with such empirical estimates be kopt=q+1k_{\mathrm{opt}}=q+1 and not qq. Indeed, the corresponding values in the table below are 0.135 versus 0.142 (q=3q=3) and 2.21e-02 versus 2.29e-02 (q=4q=4). In fact it should be observed in this example that, after koptk_{\mathrm{opt}} is reached, the average volume only slightly increases for k>koptk>k_{\mathrm{opt}}. On the contrary, until koptk_{\mathrm{opt}} is reached, the average volume is potentially much poorer.

Remark.

Even though CCLE is formulated in the standard regression framework, the presented example is essentially a time-series example. However, we do not address the typical issues encountered in conformal inference for time series, such as the balance between longitudinal and transversal coverage [31]. The analysis of our method in the time-series framework is the topic of an upcoming paper.

5.2 Cauchy data

Proposition 4.1 suggests that the confidence regions ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} may be expected to blow up in volume for heavy tailed distributions, as the limiting ellipsoid is expressed in terms of the covariance of the data, which is undefined in this case. On the contrary, since the limit sphere from the standard score Si′=‖Yi−Y^i‖2S_{i}^{\prime}=\|Y^{i}-\widehat{Y}^{i}\|^{2} have a deterministic asymptotic volume, one could expect the standard score to beat our covariance based score in terms of volume. Here we consider a central multivariate Cauchy distribution, U1∼C⁡(0,𝚺)U_{1}\sim C(0,\mathbf{\Sigma}) [27], where 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} is the same as that of Section 5.1, i.e. 𝚺i​j=k3/2​(i−j),σ2=1,L=5\mathbf{\Sigma}_{ij}=k_{3/2}(i-j),\ \sigma^{2}=1,\ L=5 (𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} cannot be interpreted as a covariance matrix anymore). In particular, C⁡(0,𝚺)C(0,\mathbf{\Sigma}) is an elliptical distribution. The numerical results are given in Figure 4, which corresponds to nsplit=3×106,ncalib=104,ntest=800n_{\mathrm{split}}=3\times 10^{6},\ n_{\mathrm{calib}}=10^{4},\ n_{\mathrm{test}}=800 and nhisto=103n_{\mathrm{histo}}=10^{3} (we have used high values for nsplitn_{\mathrm{split}} and ncalibn_{\mathrm{calib}}, hoping that the corresponding numerical simulations may illustrate a form of convergence of our method for Cauchy data). For these parameters, we see that our method still exhibits an empirical average volume of 𝔼^nhisto​𝔼^ntest​[Vol⁡(ℰαncalib)]≃790\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n_{\mathrm{histo}}}\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n_{\mathrm{test}}}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n_{\mathrm{calib}}})]\simeq 790, whereas that of the residual score is 𝔼^nhisto​𝔼^ntest​[Vol⁡(ℬαncalib)]≃1560\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n_{\mathrm{histo}}}\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n_{\mathrm{test}}}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{n_{\mathrm{calib}}})]\simeq 1560. Interestingly, these volumes also seem to exhibit a form of asymptotic normality, suggesting that ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} is indeed robust to distributions with infinite variance.

It also seems that our method is able to recover the matrix 𝚺/𝚺11\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11} (which dictates the dispersion of R1−𝚺21​(𝚺21)−1​X1R_{1}-\mathbf{\Sigma}^{21}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{21})^{-1}X_{1}), as the shape and orientation of the ellipsoid for Cauchy data is similar to that of the ellipsoid for Gaussian data (Figures 1 and 3). We refer to Appendix A.3 for further comments on this behaviour. Of course, the volumes for the Cauchy distribution are several orders of magnitude larger than that of the Gaussian data, but this is expected as Cauchy distributions are heavy tailed.

Let us turn to ℱαn\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{n} : because Cauchy data are heavy-tailed and Proposition 3.7 assumes a finite 4​qth4q^{\mathrm{th}} moment, we expect that arbitrarily large ellipsoids occur even in the regime of large ncalibn_{\mathrm{calib}} (for example we obtained 9 full space ellipsoids out of 200×500=105200\times 500=10^{5} tests, for ncalib=1000n_{\mathrm{calib}}=1000). For heavy-tailed distributions, histograms are not easily interpreted because of the large disparity of the observed values. Instead we present in Table 3 with empirical quantiles of the distribution of 𝔼^ntest​[Vol⁡(ℱαncalib)]\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n_{\mathrm{test}}}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{n_{\mathrm{calib}}})] compared to those of 𝔼^ntest​[Vol⁡(ℬαncalib)]\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n_{\mathrm{test}}}[\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{n_{\mathrm{calib}}})], as a function of ncalibn_{\mathrm{calib}}. This table shows that, from a quantile point of view, the use of ℱαn\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{n} is increasingly interesting as ncalibn_{\mathrm{calib}} increases, although empirical mean and variance still suffer from the heavy-tailed nature of Cauchy distributions. Note that ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} does not seem to suffer from this property, as shown in Figure 4 (and as could be conjectured from Proposition 3.1 and Lemma 3.5).

In this section we assume that the distribution of (X1⊤​Y1⊤)⊤(X_{1}^{\top}\ Y_{1}^{\top})^{\top} is supported on the positive orthant ℝ+p\mathbb{R}_{+}^{p}, with a density of the form

f⁡(v)∝1(1+|v|1)b+|a|1​∏i=1pviai−1,v∈ℝ+p.\displaystyle f(v)\propto\frac{1}{(1+|v|_{1})^{b+|a|_{1}}}\prod_{i=1}^{p}v_{i}^{a_{i}-1},\ \ \ v\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{p}. (87)

In equation (87), b>0b>0, (a1,…,ap)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{p}) is a vector of parameters with ai>0a_{i}>0, and |x|1=∑i=1p|xi||x|_{1}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}|x_{i}|. V1V_{1} is said to follow the inverted Dirichlet distribution which we denote by V1∼IDirichlet​(a1,…,ap,b)V_{1}\sim\text{IDirichlet}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{p};b) ([40], Example 8.6). Depending on its parameters, this distribution is mildly to heavily non elliptical, as is visible from FIgure 5. Observe also that bb controls the decay of the distribution. We next use a linear regressor trained on nsplit=5000n_{\mathrm{split}}=5000 examples. Practical experiments show that our method is efficient when the distribution of V1V_{1} is approximately elliptical. This can be seen in Figure 6, which corresponds to k=1,ℓ=3k=1,\ \ell=3, b=3b=3 and a=(1,1,10−1,10−2)a=(1,1,10^{-1},10^{-2}). Its bottom histograms show that for this distribution, the volume of ℱαn\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{n} is in average much than that of ℬαn\mathcal{B}_{\alpha}^{n}. A sample corresponding to this histogram is given in Figure 5, subfigures (a) and (b). These figures show that the set ℱαn\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{n} was able to capture part of the directionality associated to the parameters bb and aa above. We next consider an unfavourable case, where b=1b=1 and a=10−2×(1,1,1,1)a=10^{-2}\times(1,1,1,1). A sample example in given in Figure 5, subfigures (c) and (d). This figure shows that the calibration residuals are, for the most part, oriented along one of the three x,yx,y or zz axes. on this example, compared to the ball BαnB_{\alpha}^{n}, the ellipsoid ℱαn\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{n} seems to be overly sensitive to the observation of X1X_{1}. As for the Cauchy data (Table 3), unfavourable test cases are best studied with a table of empirical quantiles which we provide in Table 4. This table shows that, even for ncalib=104n_{\mathrm{calib}}=10^{4}, CCLE is severely outperformed by the norm-residual score (at least two order of magnitudes between corresponding quantiles, even for the empirical quantile of order 0.10.1).

6 Conclusion

In this article, we have introduced two covariance based scores, for conformal inference in multivariate regression. We have shown that the resulting confidence regions are conservatively and accurately approximated with an explicit ellipsoid. We have also studied their asymptotic properties, and compared them with the regions stemming from the standard conformal score function (norm of the residual) as used in the literature. Our first set of numerical experiments shows that our scores typically perform better than that of the standard norm score, in the sense that the corresponding volume is typically much lower than that of the spheres associated with the residual norm score, provided that the residuals Ri=Yi−Y^iR_{i}=Y_{i}-\widehat{Y}_{i} are not uncorrelated with the input XiX_{i}. The next step will be to apply our methodology on time series, where the adaptivity of our score function may be expected to improve the performance of CI for time series, especially concerning the longitudinal coverage (coverage within a single sample of the time series); this study will be accompanied by a Python package. We will soon extend our methodology to functional data [19]. Finally, a limitation of our scoring rule is that is may not be expected to be optimal for multimodal or non elliptical distributions of the residuals: the shape of 𝒞~αn\widetilde{\mathcal{C}}_{\alpha}^{n} is bound to be an ellipsoid. As such, generalizations of our score may be sought to include moments of order 33, to take asymmetry into account, although the matrix algebra may become intractable.

Appendix A Additional remarks

A.1 Interpretations of the score vector diag​(𝐒​(z))\text{diag}(\mathbf{S}(z))

Leverage score

Consider a multivariate linear model between the matrices 𝐑\mathbf{R} and 𝐗\mathbf{X}, 𝐑=𝐗​β+ε\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{X}\beta+\varepsilon. The ridge estimator in this linear regression model is β^=(𝐗⊤​𝐗+μ​𝐈)−1​𝐗⊤​𝐑\widehat{\beta}=(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}+\mu\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{R}. Let us denote 𝐑^=𝐗​β^=𝐗​(𝐗⊤​𝐗+μ​𝐈)−1​𝐗⊤​𝐑=𝐌𝐑\widehat{\mathbf{R}}=\mathbf{X}\widehat{\beta}=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}+\mu\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{M}\mathbf{R}. The leverage score of the i​thi\textsuperscript{th} example is the diagonal coefficient 𝐌i​i∈[0,1]\mathbf{M}_{ii}\in[0,1]. As M=∇RR^M=\nabla_{R}\widehat{R}, the leverage score can be interpreted as a self-influence score. A high leverage score Mi​iM_{ii} means that the i​thi\textsuperscript{th} example (Xi,Ri)(X_{i},R_{i}) is very influential in the behaviour of the linear model [25, 8]. The leverage score has been used, for example, for outliers detection [8]. This last task can also be tackled using conformal inference [5]. Note further that the leverage score does not depend on any underlying model nor on YY. Hence, no observational model is required for computing the leverage score. Our score is thus a form of leverage score, where we replaced the matrix 𝐌\mathbf{M} by 𝐌′=𝐖​(𝐖⊤​𝐖+μ​𝐈p)−1​𝐖⊤\mathbf{M}^{\prime}=\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{W}^{\top}\mathbf{W}+\mu\mathbf{I}_{p})^{-1}\mathbf{W}^{\top}. Hence, we jointly consider both the explanatory variables and the residual errors in the leverage score. Further, there is another difference with the classical leverage score in the centering step, as we consider 𝐖\mathbf{W} instead of 𝐕\mathbf{V}.

Shape theory

In shape theory [15], iid random vectors are observed and stacked, say row-wise, in a matrix 𝐕\mathbf{V}. In shape theory, one then typically studies the rectangular matrix 𝐕\mathbf{V} according to its polar decomposition, 𝐕=𝐏𝐓\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{T}, where 𝐓\mathbf{T} is the modulus and 𝐏\mathbf{P} is the orientation (𝐓=(𝐕⊤​𝐕)1/2\mathbf{T}=(\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{V})^{1/2} and 𝐏=𝐕(𝐕⊤𝐕)−1/2\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{V})^{-1/2}). The matrices 𝐏\mathbf{P} and 𝐓\mathbf{T} are then studied separately ([14], [9], Section 1.3.3). In particular, the random orthogonal projector 𝐏𝐏⊤\mathbf{P}\mathbf{P}^{\top} is an orientation statistic [9], Section 1.3.3, encoding directional information of the data. In our case, when λ=0\lambda=0, the connection between our score (12) and the orientation statistic 𝐏𝐏⊤\mathbf{P}\mathbf{P}^{\top} is the equality 𝐕​(𝐕⊤​𝐕)−1​𝐕⊤=𝐏𝐏⊤\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{V})^{-1}\mathbf{V}^{\top}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{P}^{\top}. As for the leverage score though, the data is usually not centered in shape theory: our score in equation (12) is, when λ=0\lambda=0, n−1​𝐒=𝐖​(𝐖⊤​𝐖)−1​𝐖⊤≠𝐕​(𝐕⊤​𝐕)−1​𝐕⊤n^{-1}\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{W}(\mathbf{W}^{\top}\mathbf{W})^{-1}\mathbf{W}^{\top}\neq\mathbf{V}(\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{V})^{-1}\mathbf{V}^{\top}. In our framework the centering step is useful to deal with potentially biased predictors f^\widehat{f}, i.e. non centered residuals.

A.2 Different assumptions for Proposition 3.4

The case λ=0\lambda=0

Our proof of Proposition 3.4 uses the fact that λ>0\lambda>0 (equation (137)): if λ=0\lambda=0, we should require that min⁡Spec⁡(𝚺)>0\min\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbf{\Sigma})>0. However, even if we can show that min⁡Spec⁡(𝚺^n)\min\mathrm{Spec}(\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n}) tends to min⁡Spec⁡(𝚺)\min\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbf{\Sigma}) almost surely (proof of Proposition 4.1), adapting the proof of Proposition 3.4 to λ=0\lambda=0 would require the control of the moments of min⁡Spec​(𝚺^n)−1\min\mathrm{Spec}(\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n})^{-1}, which is a difficult task in itself. We leave the details of the corresponding proof to the interested reader, e.g. using that almost surely, min⁡Spec⁡(𝚺^n,0)→min⁡Spec⁡(𝚺)\min\mathrm{Spec}(\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,0})\rightarrow\min\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbf{\Sigma}), from the SLLN on 𝚺^n,0\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n,0} and the continuity of the spectrum for symmetric matrices (see e.g. [20, Problem 1, p. 198]).

The assumption that 𝔼⁡[‖V1‖4​q]<+∞\mathbb{E}[\|V_{1}\|^{4q}]<+\infty (which is also used in several other places) enables us to use Jensen’s inequality, to show that supz∈Kmax1≤i≤n⁡n​bin​(z)2→0\sup_{z\in K}\max_{1\leq i\leq n}nb_{i}^{n}(z)^{2}\rightarrow 0 in probability. Under the weaker assumption that 𝔼⁡[‖V1‖2]<+∞\mathbb{E}[\|V_{1}\|^{2}]<+\infty, we can still show that the first nn coordinates of bnb^{n} verify n​∑i=1nbin​(z)2=(1+‖z‖2)​Oℙ​(1)n\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}^{n}(z)^{2}=(1+\|z\|^{2})O_{\mathbb{P}}(1), where the Oℙ​(1)O_{\mathbb{P}}(1) term is uniform in zz (e.g. adapt equation (164)). ρα,∞δ\displaystyle\frac{\rho_{\alpha,\infty}}{\delta} =1δ​q1−α​(Vc⊤​𝚺λ−1​Vc)−1δ​Xc⊤​(𝚺λ11)−1​Xc\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\delta}q_{1-\alpha}(V_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{-1}V_{\mathrm{c}})-\frac{1}{\delta}X_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{11})^{-1}X_{\mathrm{c}}
=q1−α​(Vc⊤​(δ​𝚺λ)−1​Vc)−Xc⊤​(δ​𝚺λ11)−1​Xc,\displaystyle=q_{1-\alpha}(V_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}(\delta\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda})^{-1}V_{\mathrm{c}})-X_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}(\delta\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}^{11})^{-1}X_{\mathrm{c}}, (88)

so that the product ρα,∞​𝓐∞=(δ−1​ρα,∞)​(δ​𝓐∞)\rho_{\alpha,\infty}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty}=(\delta^{-1}\rho_{\alpha,\infty})(\delta\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty}) is also unchanged when 𝚺λ\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda} is replaced with δ​𝚺λ\delta\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda}. Hence, following equation (57), ℰα​(𝚺λ,V1)=ℰα​(δ​𝚺λ,V1)\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda},V_{1})=\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}(\delta\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\lambda},V_{1}). This scaling invariance is, in fact, a key property for building the Tyler dispersion matrix estimator [46] (see equation (71) and its comments for the dispersion matrix), which is known to be robust to infinite variance in the case of elliptical distributions. The same scaling arguments can also be made for ℱα∞\mathcal{F}_{\alpha}^{\infty}, but the convergence of ρn,α′\rho_{n,\alpha}^{\prime} to q1−αℱq_{1-\alpha}^{\mathcal{F}} is not at all clear (see e.g. the assumptions of Proposition 4.3), as can be seen from the numerical experiments with Cauchy data. The further study of our method for heavy-tailed data is left for future work.

A.4 Non asymptotic analysis in the Gaussian case

One may wish to understand the properties of ℰαn\mathcal{E}_{\alpha}^{n} for finite sample size nn. For example, assuming that λ=0\lambda=0, it is known that 𝓐n=𝚺^n/𝚺^n11\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{n}=\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n}/\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n}^{11} follows the Wishart distribution Wℓ​(n−k−1,n−1​𝚺/𝚺11)W_{\ell}(n-k-1,n^{-1}\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11}) [39], Theorem 3.2.10. We now turn to the quantities appearing in ρn,α\rho_{n,\alpha}. Observing that n/(n+1)​Xn+1c∼𝒩⁡(0,𝚺11)\sqrt{n/(n+1)}X_{n+1}^{\mathrm{c}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11}), that n​𝚺^n11∼Wk​(n−1,𝚺11)n\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n}^{11}\sim W_{k}(n-1,\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11}) and that both are independent [34], Corollary 3.3.3.2, we obtain that [(n−1)/(n+1)]​(Xcn+1)⊤​(𝚺^n11)−1​Xn+1c[(n-1)/(n+1)](X^{n+1}_{\mathrm{c}})^{\top}(\widehat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{n}^{11})^{-1}X_{n+1}^{\mathrm{c}} follows the Hotelling T2T^{2} distribution T2​(k,n−1)T^{2}(k,n-1) [34], Theorem 3.5.1. Let us now also assume that 𝔼⁡[V1]\mathbb{E}[V_{1}] is known. In this case, it is reasonable to replace n−1​∑i=1nVin^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}V_{i} with 𝔼⁡[V1]\mathbb{E}[V_{1}] in 𝐁n\mathbf{B}_{n} (equation (21)), so that 𝐁n\mathbf{B}_{n} follows the matrix normal distribution 𝐁n∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈n,𝚺)\mathbf{B}_{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{n},\mathbf{\Sigma}) [9], Section 1.5.3. In this case, 𝐏n,0\mathbf{P}_{n,0} is a random orthogonal projector whose distribution is uniform over the so-called “special manifold” 𝐏p,n−p⊂ℳn,n\mathbf{P}_{p,n-p}\subset\mathcal{M}_{n,n} of orthogonal projectors of rank pp, which is isomorphic to the Grassmanian manifold Gp,nG_{p,n} [9], Theorem 2.4.9. Finally, building on [39], Exercise 3.15 p. 117, we can show that (𝐏n,0)i​i({\mathbf{P}_{n,0}})_{ii} follows a Beta distribution B⁡(p/2,(n−p)/2)B(p/2,(n-p)/2). Note though that those results, while instructive, are not sufficient to describe the distribution of ρn,α\rho_{n,\alpha}.

When 𝔼⁡[V1]\mathbb{E}[V_{1}] is unknown, we expect to obtain perturbations of the distributions above for 𝐏n,0\mathbf{P}_{n,0} and (𝐏n,0)i​i({\mathbf{P}_{n,0}})_{ii}. Still, to our knowledge, there are no simple expressions available in this case. Indeed, the procedure for building 𝐁n\mathbf{B}_{n} correlates the columns of 𝐁n\mathbf{B}_{n} through equation (94), and 𝐁n∼𝒩⁡(0,π𝟙⟂,𝚺)\mathbf{B}_{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\pi^{\perp}_{\mathbbm{1}},\mathbf{\Sigma}) (here, 𝟙∈ℝn\mathbbm{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}). As such, the distribution of 𝐏n,0\mathbf{P}_{n,0} does not seem to be available in closed form since neither π𝟙⟂\pi^{\perp}_{\mathbbm{1}} nor 𝚺\mathbf{\Sigma} are equal to the identity matrix [9], Chapter 2.

The core idea for this result is the observation that for all z∈Kz\in K,

Proof of Lemma 3.5.

From equation (32) and observing that 0≼𝐏n,λ≼𝐏n,00\preccurlyeq\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda}\preccurlyeq\mathbf{P}_{n,0}, we may first write that

Tr​(𝐏n,λ)≤Tr​(𝐏n,0)≤p.\displaystyle\text{Tr}(\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda})\leq\text{Tr}(\mathbf{P}_{n,0})\leq p. (146)

Now, denote p(i)p_{(i)} the i​thi\textsuperscript{th} order statistic of (p1,n,…,pn,n)(p_{1,n},\dots,p_{n,n}), p(1)≤⋯≤p(n)p_{(1)}\leq\dots\leq p_{(n)}. Then

Tr​(𝐏n,λ)=∑i=1npi,n=∑i=1np(i)≥∑i=nαnp(i)≥p(nα)​(n+1−nα)=qn,αn​(n+1−nα).\displaystyle\text{Tr}(\mathbf{P}_{n,\lambda})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{i,n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{(i)}\geq\sum_{i=n_{\alpha}}^{n}p_{(i)}\geq p_{(n_{\alpha})}(n+1-n_{\alpha})=\frac{q_{n,\alpha}}{n}(n+1-n_{\alpha}). (147)

Moreover,

n+1−nα\displaystyle n+1-n_{\alpha} =n+1−⌈(1−α)​(n+1)⌉=n+1+⌊−(1−α)​(n+1)⌋\displaystyle=n+1-\lceil(1-\alpha)(n+1)\rceil=n+1+\lfloor-(1-\alpha)(n+1)\rfloor
=⌊n+1−(1−α)​(n+1)⌋=⌊α⁡(n+1)⌋.\displaystyle=\lfloor n+1-(1-\alpha)(n+1)\rfloor=\lfloor\alpha(n+1)\rfloor. (148)

Thus, combining equations (146), (147) and (148),

qn,α≤n​pn+1−nα=n​p⌊α⁡(n+1)⌋.\displaystyle q_{n,\alpha}\leq\frac{np}{n+1-n_{\alpha}}=\frac{np}{\lfloor\alpha(n+1)\rfloor}. (149)

Hence, a sufficient condition for qn,α<n−1q_{n,\alpha}<n-1 is n​p/⌊α⁡(n+1)⌋<n−1np/\lfloor\alpha(n+1)\rfloor<n-1, that is,

n​pn−1<⌊α⁡(n+1)⌋.\displaystyle\frac{np}{n-1}<\lfloor\alpha(n+1)\rfloor. (150)

But this is equivalent to ⌊n​p/(n−1)⌋+1≤⌊α⁡(n+1)⌋\lfloor{np}/({n-1})\rfloor+1\leq\lfloor\alpha(n+1)\rfloor, which is also equivalent to

⌊n​pn−1⌋+1=p+⌊pn−1⌋+1\displaystyle\bigg\lfloor\frac{np}{n-1}\bigg\rfloor+1=p+\bigg\lfloor\frac{p}{n-1}\bigg\rfloor+1 ≤α⁡(n+1).\displaystyle\leq\alpha(n+1). (151)

Thus, if p<n−1p<n-1, then ⌊p/(n−1)⌋=0\lfloor{p}/(n-1)\rfloor=0 and we obtain the sufficient condition α≥(p+1)/(n+1)\alpha\geq(p+1)/(n+1). ∎

But, when s→+∞s\rightarrow+\infty and qq is fixed, Γ⁡(s+q)/Γ⁡(s)∼sq\Gamma(s+q)/\Gamma(s)\sim s^{q} ([1], Section 6.1.39). In particular, this proves equation (61). ∎

=det(𝚺)−1/2∫ℝk∫ℝℓh((𝚺/𝚺11)−1/2w)g((u−μu)⊤(𝚺11)−1(u−μu)+w⊤(𝚺/𝚺11)−1w)dvdu\displaystyle=\det(\mathbf{\Sigma})^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{\ell}}h((\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1/2}w)g((u-\mu_{u})^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}(u-\mu_{u})+w^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}w)dvdu (209)
=det(𝚺)−1/2det(𝚺/𝚺11)1/2∫ℝk∫ℝℓh(z)g((u−μu)⊤(𝚺11)−1(u−μu)+∥z∥2)dzdu\displaystyle=\det(\mathbf{\Sigma})^{-1/2}\det(\mathbf{\Sigma}/\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{1/2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{\ell}}h(z)g((u-\mu_{u})^{\top}(\mathbf{\Sigma}^{11})^{-1}(u-\mu_{u})+\|z\|^{2})dzdu (210)
=∫ℝℓh⁡(z)​(∫ℝkg⁡(‖x‖2+‖z‖2)​𝑑x)​𝑑z.\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{\ell}}h(z)\bigg(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}g(\|x\|^{2}+\|z\|^{2})dx\bigg)dz. (211)

‖Z‖2=d‖Y‖2.\displaystyle\|Z\|^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}\|Y\|^{2}. (212)

Tc⊤​𝓐∞−1​Tc=d∑i=1ℓTi2,and‖R1‖2=d∑i=1ℓλi​(Ti+si)2,\displaystyle T_{\mathrm{c}}^{\top}\bm{\mathcal{A}}_{\infty}^{-1}T_{\mathrm{c}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}T_{i}^{2},\ \ \ \text{and}\ \ \ \|R_{1}\|^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\lambda_{i}(T_{i}+s_{i})^{2},

for some vector s∈ℝℓs\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell} and where the λi\lambda_{i} are the eignevalues of 𝚺22\mathbf{\Sigma}^{22}. ≤q1−α​(∑i=1ℓTi2)q1−α​(∑i=1ℓδi​(Ti+si)2).\displaystyle\leq\frac{q_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}T_{i}^{2})}{q_{1-\alpha}(\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\delta_{i}(T_{i}+s_{i})^{2})}. (214)

gY​(r)−gY​(r′)=∫ℝkg⁡(‖x‖2+r)−g⁡(‖x‖2+r′)​𝑑x≥0.\displaystyle g_{Y}(r)-g_{Y}(r^{\prime})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}g(\|x\|^{2}+r)-g(\|x\|^{2}+r^{\prime})dx\geq 0.

Proof of Proposition 4.11.

For all ii, define δi≔λi/(λ1⋯λℓ)1/ℓ\delta_{i}\coloneqq\lambda_{i}/(\lambda_{1}\cdots\lambda_{\ell})^{1/\ell} and (G1,…,Gℓ)(G_{1},\ldots,G_{\ell}) to be a random vector with independent components, such that GiG_{i} follows the gamma distribution γ⁡(δi,δi−1)\gamma(\delta_{i},\delta_{i}^{-1}).
